Everything per-tenant is either derived by the operators or rendered from the tenant list by the Template Operator, never authored. The eleventh tenant costs nothing, where by hand it would cost another sixteen.

More valuable than the saving is that two definitions cannot disagree when there is only one. The gateways and the Grafana extension watch Tenant resources, and the Template Operator renders from them, so what observability enforces tracks what the cluster grants rather than tracking it at whatever interval someone remembers to reconcile the two. A tenant removed from Kubernetes cannot be left behind with an organisation that still queries its old data — the characteristic failure of a hand-maintained tenant list.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  subgraph K["Kubernetes"]
    T["<b>Tenant</b> resources"]
    API["API server<br/>TokenReview · SubjectAccessReview"]
  end

  subgraph W["Ingestion"]
    P["Application pods<br/>in tenant namespaces"] --> C["Collector<br/>tags and routes per tenant"]
  end

  subgraph E["Gateways — authorise the caller, then set the tenant header"]
    LG["MTO Loki Gateway"]
    MG["MTO Mimir Gateway"]
    TG["Tempo Operator gateway"]
  end

  subgraph S["Storage, partitioned by tenant"]
    L[("Loki")]
    M[("Mimir")]
    TP[("Tempo")]
  end

  subgraph R["Access"]
    U["Tenant member"] -->|"OIDC login"| G[("Grafana<br/>one organisation per tenant")]
    X["Grafana extension"] -->|"organisation and<br/>tenant-scoped data sources"| G
  end

  C -->|"ServiceAccount token"| LG & MG & TG
  G -->|"ServiceAccount token"| LG & MG & TG
  LG --> L
  MG --> M
  TG --> TP
  LG & MG -.->|"verify"| API
  T -.->|"watched"| LG & MG & X
  T -.->|"read"| TO["Template Operator"]
  TO -.->|"renders per-tenant<br/>configuration"| C

Telemetry goes in through a collector and comes back out through Grafana. Both directions cross the same gateways, and the tenant is settled there rather than taken on trust.

docs.title: Getting telemetry in
docs.text:
One platform-managed collector serves the whole cluster. It derives each tenant from the namespace its source pod runs in, so workloads need no observability configuration of their own.

An OpenTelemetry Collector is the usual choice, but not the only one — the gateways accept the native protocol of each backend alongside OTLP: Prometheus remote write for metrics, Loki's push API for logs. Whatever writes must do two things: present a ServiceAccount token the gateway authorises, and name the tenant it is writing for.

That second requirement shapes how each one is configured. A collector reads the namespace from each record and routes accordingly, so a single pipeline covers every tenant. Prometheus cannot do that, because remote-write headers are fixed per block — one instance covering many namespaces, such as OpenShift's user workload monitoring, would label every series with the same tenant. It therefore needs a block per tenant, each filtered to that tenant's namespaces.

Neither is written per tenant by hand. The Template Operator that ships with MTO reads your Tenant resources and renders the per-tenant configuration — collector routes, remote-write blocks — from that one list, so the repetition is generated from the same source as everything else on this page. It can also be set to reconcile what it rendered, reverting drift.

docs.title: What settles the tenant
docs.text:
With multi-tenancy turned on, Loki, Mimir and Tempo each read the tenant from an X-Scope-OrgID header, and none of them authenticates it. All three tell you to run an authenticating reverse proxy in front, and to let that proxy set the header. Grafana's boundary is the organisation, and it has no idea which organisation belongs to which tenant. So all four need something alongside them:

Signal Component What settles the tenant Detail Logs Loki MTO Loki Gateway Authorises every request against your tenants, in place of the gateway a LokiStack would otherwise run Metrics Mimir MTO Mimir Gateway Authorises every request against your tenants. Mimir has no authenticating layer of its own Traces Tempo Tempo Operator gateway Tempo partitions traces itself; the operator's gateway authenticates and authorises per tenant Dashboards Grafana The Grafana extension Organisations, tenant-scoped data source copies, and access mapped from identity-provider groups

Both MTO gateways check a caller the same way. The request carries a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token; the gateway verifies it with the TokenReview API, confirms the tenant is one of those it watches, and authorises that caller for that tenant — against an allow-list, or Kubernetes RBAC.

Where they differ is how the tenant is named. A Loki request names it in the URL, as /api/logs/v1/{tenant}/…, and the gateway sets the header from that path, discarding whatever header and credentials the caller sent. A Mimir request names it in the header, which the gateway validates and then re-sets from the value it authorised. Either way, a caller reaches only a tenant it was authorised for.

The collector and Grafana are both such callers, each with a ServiceAccount of its own. Going in, the collector names the tenant it routed the telemetry to. Coming out, the tenant comes from the data source the extension wrote for that tenant's organisation — so which tenant a query belongs to is settled by which organisation the person is in.

Note

The MTO gateways use only standard Kubernetes APIs, so they run on any distribution — vanilla Kubernetes, EKS, GKE, AKS or OpenShift.

Warning

Tempo must run behind its gateway, and that gateway's tenants must be kept aligned with yours, because unlike the Loki and Mimir gateways it does not read Tenant resources. Tempo on its own accepts whichever tenant a request names, so the gateway is what makes the trace boundary hold.

docs.title: What it is made of
docs.text:
Most of the stack is upstream. MTO supplies the pieces that make the tenant boundary real.

Component How it can be deployed Role here Loki The Loki Operator as a LokiStack, or its Helm chart Stores logs, partitioned by tenant Mimir The mimir-distributed Helm chart Stores metrics, partitioned by tenant Tempo The Tempo Operator as a TempoStack, or the tempo-distributed chart Stores traces, partitioned by tenant, behind its gateway Collector The OpenTelemetry Operator, its Helm chart or plain manifests Tags telemetry with its source tenant and writes it through the gateways Grafana The Grafana Operator Dashboards and exploration, one organisation per tenant Template Operator Ships with MTO Renders per-tenant configuration, such as collector routes and remote-write blocks, from your Tenant resources MTO Loki Gateway, MTO Mimir Gateway Stakater Verify the caller on every Loki and Mimir request, then set the tenant header The Grafana extension Stakater Derives organisations, data sources, dashboards and access from your tenants

Where both an operator and a chart exist, either will do, and the choice can follow whatever a cluster already runs — on OpenShift that is usually the operator, since Red Hat ships its own Loki, Tempo and OpenTelemetry operators. Three components are narrower than that, for reasons worth knowing rather than working around:

  • Tempo — both routes deploy Tempo, and both ship a gateway, but the two are not equivalent. The chart's is an nginx proxy offering basic authentication, which identifies a caller without tying it to a tenant. The operator's authenticates with OIDC and authorises per tenant, which is what the trace boundary depends on.
  • Mimir — Grafana publishes the chart and no operator of its own, so the chart is the route.
  • Grafana — the extension configures an instance the Grafana Operator owns, so that operator is required rather than preferred.

Stakater can deploy the whole stack, or only the MTO components in front of an LGTM stack you already run. Either way two requirements hold: multi-tenancy must be enabled on Loki, Mimir and Tempo, and whatever collects telemetry must tag it with the source pod's namespace.

docs.title: What you can tailor
docs.text:
The tenant boundary is the part that stays constant. Most of what surrounds it is a choice, and much of it can be changed after the stack is running.

Choice Options Which signals you run Logs, metrics and traces are independent — run any combination, and add another later How telemetry is written OTLP from a collector, Prometheus remote write for metrics, or Loki's push API for logs Who deploys the stack Stakater deploys all of it, or only the MTO components in front of one you already run How callers are authorised at the gateways A ServiceAccount allow-list, or Kubernetes RBAC through SubjectAccessReview Which requests the gateways accept The standard route set for each backend, plus any extra routes you add How the Loki gateway reaches Loki TLS managed with a LokiStack, or certificates from a Secret you supply How tenant members sign in Identity-provider details from a Secret, written inline, or single sign-on turned off Which tenants receive a dashboard or data source Every tenant, or only the ones an annotation names Which group names grant which role A templated pattern per role, so one pattern covers every tenant Views across several tenants Off, or on with a choice of role, cross-tenant traces, and dashboard sharing

The last four rows — sign-in, targeting, role patterns and cross-tenant views — belong to the Grafana extension and are set on its Grafana resource. The Grafana integration page covers each in full, with field names and defaults.

One check confirms the whole chain, however you assemble it. Sign in as a member of one tenant, confirm you can see that tenant's logs, metrics and traces, then confirm a request for another tenant's data is refused.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Grafana integration — organisations, data sources, dashboards, single sign-on and cross-tenant views in full.
  • Create a tenant — the resource everything else is derived from.

docs.title: Delivery and login
docs.text: External Secrets delivers secrets to workloads as Kubernetes Secrets, and human SSO lets tenant members sign in to OpenBao.

docs.title: Delivering secrets as Kubernetes Secrets
docs.text:
Most applications should not call OpenBao at all. With the External Secrets Operator (ESO), on by default, the extension wires up delivery: ESO logs into OpenBao for the workload, fetches the secret and keeps an ordinary Kubernetes Secret in sync with it.

For each ServiceAccount you give a tier, the extension creates a SecretStore named <serviceaccount>-bao that logs in with the same role as the workload. You then request secrets with annotations on the Deployment — each produces one Kubernetes Secret, named <serviceaccount>-<name>:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-a-api
  annotations:
    bao.stakater.com/kv-secret.db-creds: postgres        # the whole secret
    bao.stakater.com/kv-secret.api-key: external#token   # just the "token" field
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: web
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: my/web:1.0
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: web-db-creds

The value is <leaf>[#<field>]: with #<field>, only that field is copied into the Secret; without it, every field becomes a key.

sequenceDiagram
    participant MTO as OpenBao extension
    participant ESO as External Secrets Operator
    participant Bao as OpenBao
    participant K8s as Kubernetes
    MTO->>ESO: SecretStore web-bao, ExternalSecret web-db-creds
    ESO->>Bao: log in with the workload's own role
    Bao-->>ESO: the secret at kv/data/dev/team-a-api/web/postgres
    ESO->>K8s: create or update Secret web-db-creds
    Note over ESO,Bao: repeats every refresh interval — 1h by default

The workload mounts the Secret and never learns OpenBao exists. Two more annotations cover the sharing cases: bao.stakater.com/kv-subscribe.<name> reads from a sibling namespace's shared folder, and bao.stakater.com/kv-import.<name> reads from another tenant (prefixed with the source, e.g. team-a-api/postgres, team-a/creds). Each needs the matching grant on the ServiceAccount — see Secrets and sharing.

Note

Every refresh is an OpenBao login. The default interval is one hour, and every workload logs in on it, so shortening the interval multiplies the load on OpenBao by the number of workloads.

docs.title: Human login
docs.text:
With sso.enabled, people sign in to OpenBao through your identity provider and their access follows their groups. For each tier, the extension creates a login role bound to an identity-provider group named <tenant>-<tier>s by default — so members of team-a-admins get the admin tier in team-a. Unlike a workload, which is confined to one namespace, a signed-in person gets that tier across the whole tenant.

sequenceDiagram
    participant MTO as OpenBao extension
    participant Bao as OpenBao
    participant IdP as OIDC provider
    participant User as Tenant member
    MTO->>Bao: create one OIDC login role per tier, bound to an IdP group
    User->>Bao: bao login -method=oidc -namespace=team-a
    Bao->>IdP: authenticate and read the group claim
    Bao-->>User: token carrying that tier's policies
    User->>Bao: read and write across the tenant
bao login -method=oidc -namespace=team-a role=sso-team-a-admin

Sessions are short — 15 minutes by default, 1 hour at most — because removing someone from a group in the identity provider does not revoke tokens already issued.

Previous: Encryption and certificates · Next: Security

docs.title: Encryption and certificates
docs.text: Two engines beyond KV: transit for encryption, PKI for certificates. Both are reached the same way as KV — one login with the ServiceAccount token, then the paths from the ConfigMap.

docs.title: Encrypting data (transit)
docs.text:
Add bao.stakater.com/transit: "true" alongside an editor or admin tier, and the workload gets three encryption keys: one private to the application, one shared by every opted-in application in its namespace, and one shared across the tenant. Keys rotate every 90 days by default and never leave OpenBao.

The ConfigMap carries each key's encrypt and decrypt endpoints, so encrypting is one call:

curl -s --request POST \
  --header "X-Vault-Token: ${VAULT_TOKEN}" \
  --header "X-Vault-Namespace: ${VAULT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --data '{"plaintext":"'"$(echo -n 'hello' | base64)"'"}' \
  "${VAULT_ADDR}/v1/${VAULT_TRANSIT_APP_ENCRYPT}"

Two workloads that must exchange encrypted data use the tenant-shared key on both sides. Across tenants, transit-export-tenant and transit-import-tenant create one key per pair: the exporter may encrypt and decrypt, the importer may only decrypt.

docs.title: Issuing certificates (PKI)
docs.text:
Each tenant gets its own certificate authority — by default an intermediate signed by a cluster-wide platform CA, so every tenant's certificates chain back to a single anchor. Trusting another tenant is still opt-in; the anchor alone grants nothing.

flowchart LR
  R["Platform CA<br/>self-signed, or signed by<br/>your own offline root"] --> A["team-a<br/>intermediate CA"]
  R --> B["team-b<br/>intermediate CA"]
  A --> AL["certificates for<br/>*.team-a-api.svc.cluster.local"]
  B --> BL["certificates for<br/>*.team-b-prod.svc.cluster.local"]

The shipped role issues certificates for *.svc.cluster.local names in the tenant's own namespaces, valid for 7 days.

docs.title: Through cert-manager (recommended)
docs.text:
Turn on parent.certManager.enabled and each opted-in namespace gets an Issuer named after the tenant's certificate role. Applications then request certificates the normal way, and the private key is generated in the cluster and never sent to OpenBao:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: web-tls
  namespace: team-a-api
spec:
  secretName: web-tls
  issuerRef:
    name: team-a-svc
    kind: Issuer
  commonName: web.team-a-api.svc.cluster.local   # required
  dnsNames:
    - web.team-a-api.svc.cluster.local

Note

commonName is not optional. A Certificate carrying only dnsNames is refused at signing time; it sits at Ready=False, and the reason appears on the CertificateRequest, not on the Certificate.

docs.title: Directly from OpenBao
docs.text: With bao.stakater.com/pki: "true" on the ServiceAccount, the ConfigMap offers two endpoints: VAULT_PKI_SIGN_PATH, where you send a certificate signing request and the private key never leaves the pod, and VAULT_PKI_ISSUE_PATH, where OpenBao generates the key and returns it over the network. Prefer signing.

docs.title: Cross-tenant trust
docs.text:
Namespaces in one tenant share a CA, so they already trust one another. Across tenants, trust is opt-in and decided by the consuming side:

  • bao.stakater.com/pki-trust-tenant — trust a peer's server certificates when you call it.
  • bao.stakater.com/pki-allow-tenant — accept that peer as a client calling you.

Accepting implies trusting; trusting never implies accepting.

Previous: Secrets and sharing · Next: Delivery and login

docs.title: Giving an application a secret
docs.text: This is the path most people take, and everything else builds on it: annotate the workload, write a secret, read it from a pod. The examples use tenant team-a and its namespace team-a-api, created the ordinary way — see Creating a tenant. Nothing about the Tenant is OpenBao-specific.

docs.title: 1. Annotate the ServiceAccount
docs.text:
The ServiceAccount is the identity OpenBao authenticates, so this is where access is granted. Name the engine you want, and the tier to grant it at:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-a-api
  annotations:
    bao.stakater.com/kv: "true"
    bao.stakater.com/tier: editor

tier is required alongside any engine — an engine annotation on its own grants nothing. For ServiceAccount web, this creates:

  • an OpenBao policy scoped to that application's own path, kv/data/dev/team-a-api/web/*;
  • a Kubernetes auth role, so the pod can trade its ServiceAccount token for a short-lived OpenBao token;
  • a ConfigMap named bao-config-web in team-a-api, holding every address, role and path the workload needs.

The last path segment is the application, which defaults to the ServiceAccount name. Scoping to the application rather than the namespace is what stops two workloads in one namespace reading each other's secrets.

sequenceDiagram
    participant MTO as OpenBao extension
    participant K8s as Kubernetes
    participant Bao as OpenBao
    participant Pod
    MTO->>K8s: watch ServiceAccounts annotated bao.stakater.com/*
    MTO->>Bao: create the policy and login role for this ServiceAccount
    MTO->>K8s: write the bao-config-web ConfigMap beside the workload
    Pod->>Bao: log in with its ServiceAccount token
    Bao->>K8s: verify the token
    Bao-->>Pod: short-lived token carrying the application's policy
    Pod->>Bao: read and write under its own path

docs.title: 2. Write the first secret
docs.text:
Someone has to write the first secret, which means knowing the path. The bao-apps ConfigMap answers that — every namespace with at least one OpenBao-enabled ServiceAccount has one, an entry per application:

$ kubectl get cm bao-apps -n team-a-api -o jsonpath='{.data.web}'
serviceAccount: "web"
tier: "editor"
engines: kv
kvPath: kv/data/dev/team-a-api/web/

A person signed in through OIDC, or a pipeline with its own credentials, writes to that path:

bao login -method=oidc -namespace=team-a role=sso-team-a-admin
bao kv put -mount=kv dev/team-a-api/web/postgres username=app password=s3cr3t

In the OpenBao web UI, open the kv mount and browse dev/team-a-api/web/. The /data/ segment in kvPath is an API artefact and does not appear in the UI.

docs.title: 3. Read the secret from the pod
docs.text:
Load the ConfigMap into the pod, and everything the workload needs is in its environment:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-a-api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: web
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: my/web:1.0
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: bao-config-web

export VAULT_TOKEN=$(bao write -field=token auth/kubernetes/login \
  role="${VAULT_K8S_ROLE}" \
  jwt=@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)

bao read "${VAULT_KV_APP_PATH}postgres"

The ConfigMap always carries the server address, the tenant's OpenBao namespace, the login role and the application's own paths:

Key Example Meaning VAULT_ADDR https://openbao.openbao:8200 OpenBao server URL VAULT_NAMESPACE team-a/ the tenant's OpenBao namespace VAULT_K8S_ROLE team-a-team-a-api-web the login role for this ServiceAccount VAULT_KV_APP_PATH kv/data/dev/team-a-api/web/ where this application's secrets live VAULT_KV_SHARED_OUT_PATH kv/data/dev/_shared/from-team-a-api/ the namespace's shared folder

Read these from the ConfigMap rather than copying them into manifests — they differ per tenant and application. Transit and PKI add their own keys when enabled.

Note

Every engine is reached the same way: one login with the ServiceAccount token, then the paths from the ConfigMap. Once you know it, transit and PKI need nothing new.

docs.title: Prefer delivery over in-app calls
docs.text:
Most applications should not call OpenBao at all — annotate the Deployment and the secret arrives as a Kubernetes Secret through External Secrets. See Delivery and login. Use the in-pod calls above only when an app genuinely needs the OpenBao API.

Previous: Installation · Next: Secrets and sharing

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Done once per cluster, by a platform administrator, before any tenant gets an OpenBao namespace. There is no per-tenant installation step.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An OpenBao server reachable from the cluster.
  • Template Operator v2 (templates.v2.stakater.com) and the OpenBao Config Operator — the extension renders objects for them and does nothing without them.
  • External Secrets Operator, while secrets are delivered as Kubernetes Secrets (the default).
  • cert-manager to issue certificates through Kubernetes, and trust-manager for trust between tenants.
  • An OIDC identity provider, for human login.

MTO labels each tenant namespace stakater.com/tenant=<tenant-name>, and the extension uses that label to find them.

docs.title: Install Template Operator v2
docs.text: The simplest route is to let MTO deploy it: set components.templateOperatorV2.mode: Managed in the IntegrationConfig. MTO then runs it in multi-tenant-operator as the ServiceAccount tenant-operator-template-operator-v2.

docs.title: Install the OpenBao Config Operator
docs.text:
The OpenBao Config Operator applies to OpenBao the custom resources the extension renders. Install it once per cluster.

On plain Kubernetes, apply the release manifest (server-side, because the bundled CRDs are large):

kubectl apply --server-side -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stakater/openbao-config-operator/v0.0.6/dist/install.yaml

It runs in the openbao-config-operator-system namespace. On OpenShift, install it from its OLM catalog instead — a CatalogSource and a Subscription; see the operator's deployment guide.

The operator holds no OpenBao token: it authenticates with its own ServiceAccount through the one-time bootstrap in Give the operator its own credentials below.

docs.title: Enable the extension
docs.text:
The extension is installed once per cluster with Helm; it watches Tenant resources cluster-wide and renders one set of configuration per tenant, which the OpenBao Config Operator applies.

A tenant is picked up once its spec lists at least one namespace under withTenantPrefix or withoutTenantPrefix. The check reads those two fields and nothing else: sandboxes do not count, and neither do namespaces attached by label alone — a Tenant listing none is skipped, silently, even when labelled namespaces exist. Add one and it is picked up on the next render.

Everything under parent is passed to every tenant — this is where you point the cluster at your OpenBao server and choose which features are on:

parent:
  baoServer: https://openbao.openbao.svc.cluster.local:8200
  env: dev                    # a segment in every secret path, so one server can hold several environments
  eso: enabled                # deliver secrets as Kubernetes Secrets
  certManager:
    enabled: false            # cert-manager Issuers per namespace
  sso:
    enabled: false            # human login through OIDC
    issuerUrl: ""

Values outside parent cover the cluster's own setup rather than the tenants': platformPki for the certificate authority that signs each tenant's CA, and safety for what deletion does. The certificate roles tenants issue from are install-wide too, under parent.pki.roles. What each tier may do is fixed by the extension and is not a value.

docs.title: Give the operator its own credentials
docs.text:
The OpenBao Config Operator authenticates to OpenBao with its own Kubernetes ServiceAccount and stores no token anywhere. This needs a one-time bootstrap per OpenBao server: an auth mount for the cluster, a policy covering what the operator manages, and a role binding that policy to the operator's ServiceAccount.

Warning

Never give the operator OpenBao's root token. In production, set baoServer to an https:// address, and set baoCABundle if OpenBao serves with a private CA.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n openbao-config-operator-system \
  get templateinstances.templates.v2.stakater.com openbao-config-mto-parent \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.outputs.tiReady}' | jq .

Anything other than True for a tenant means its configuration did not reach OpenBao — see Operating. Then confirm the OpenBao namespaces exist, one per tenant.

Tip

Always use the fully-qualified templateinstances.templates.v2.stakater.com. On OpenShift a bare kubectl get templateinstance returns OpenShift's own kind with an empty status.

Previous: Overview · Next: Giving an application a secret

docs.title: Operating
docs.text: Day-2 for a platform administrator: check what was created, diagnose a workload that cannot log in, and understand what deletion does.

docs.title: Checking what was created
docs.text:
For tenant team-a, the resources the extension renders:

kubectl -n openbao-config-operator-system get \
  obns,obse,obam,obkac,obkar,obp,obtk,obpkic,obpkir \
  -l templates.v2.stakater.com/instance=openbao-config-mto-team-a

One read covers the health of every tenant at once:

kubectl -n openbao-config-operator-system \
  get templateinstances.templates.v2.stakater.com openbao-config-mto-parent \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.outputs.tiReady}' | jq .

Anything other than True for a tenant means its configuration did not reach OpenBao. The neighbouring tiRendered and tiApplied fields say whether it failed to render or was refused on apply.

Tip

Always use the fully-qualified templateinstances.templates.v2.stakater.com. On OpenShift a bare kubectl get templateinstance returns OpenShift's own kind with an empty status — indistinguishable from "nothing is reconciling".

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
A workload cannot log in. In order:

  • The ServiceAccount needs both an engine annotation and bao.stakater.com/tier — an engine on its own grants nothing.
  • Annotation values are strings — "true" must be quoted, or Kubernetes rejects it as a boolean.
  • The bao-config-<serviceaccount> ConfigMap appears only once the ServiceAccount is annotated. If it is missing, the annotation has not been picked up.
  • Grants go on the ServiceAccount and secret requests on the Deployment. A key on the wrong object is reported as an error beside the workload, not ignored.

A whole tenant is missing. Check its Tenant lists a namespace under withTenantPrefix or withoutTenantPrefix — a tenant listing none is skipped, silently — and that its namespaces carry stakater.com/tenant=<tenant-name>.

docs.title: What deletion does
docs.text:
Deleting a resource does not destroy the data behind it, by default.

What is deleted What happens An engine, an OpenBao namespace or an auth mount Retained. The OpenBao object and everything under it survives; re-creating an identical resource adopts it back. A policy, login role, group or alias Deleted, so the access it granted is revoked.

The practical consequence: deleting an MTO Tenant does not destroy its OpenBao data. Its secrets, encryption keys and certificate authority are retained while its policies and login roles are removed, so access closes but the data is recoverable by re-creating the tenant.

Warning

To remove a tenant's data for real, delete the tenant and then, with an OpenBao administrator token, delete its OpenBao namespace — bao namespace delete <tenant> cascades through everything inside it.

Removing an annotation from a ServiceAccount revokes what it granted, so access follows the workload definition rather than lingering in OpenBao.

Previous: Security · Next: Reference

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
OpenBao is an identity-based secret and encryption management system. With the Multi-Tenant Operator (MTO), the OpenBao extension gives every tenant its own OpenBao namespace — a secrets store, encryption keys and a certificate authority — with the policies and login roles that let the tenant's people and workloads reach them and nothing else, all derived from the Tenant you already maintain.

Note

This is the Helm-chart OpenBao extension (mto-extension-openbao). It is optional.

Requires Template Operator v2 and the OpenBao Config Operator

The extension is configuration — it installs no controller of its own. It renders Template Operator v2 objects (templates.v2.stakater.com), which render OpenBao Config Operator custom resources; that operator applies them to OpenBao. Both operators must be running. See Installation.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
You maintain The extension keeps in sync a Tenant an OpenBao namespace per tenant — KV, transit and PKI inside it a ServiceAccount annotation per app a policy + login role scoped to that app's own path a Deployment annotation the secret delivered as a Kubernetes Secret via External Secrets

Everything an application team writes fits on one screen — the ServiceAccount says what the app needs, the Deployment says which secret to deliver, and the container reads an ordinary Kubernetes Secret:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-a-api
  annotations:
    bao.stakater.com/kv: "true"       # give this application a private secrets path
    bao.stakater.com/tier: editor     # it may read and write there
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: team-a-api
  annotations:
    bao.stakater.com/kv-secret.db-creds: postgres   # deliver this secret
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: web
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: my/web:1.0
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: web-db-creds    # created and kept in sync for you

The OpenBao policy, the login role and the Kubernetes Secret are all created from those three annotations. A developer never writes an OpenBao policy and never holds a static credential — the pod authenticates with the token Kubernetes already gives it.

docs.title: What each tenant gets
docs.text:
Capability Default What it is A private OpenBao namespace on Everything for the tenant lives under <tenant>/. One tenant cannot see or reach another tenant's. Secrets storage on A KV engine (v2), each application's secrets on its own path. Encryption keys on A transit engine — the workload sends data and gets it back encrypted; the key never leaves OpenBao. Certificates on A PKI certificate authority per tenant, for serving TLS and service-to-service mTLS. Secret delivery on Secrets arrive as Kubernetes Secrets through External Secrets, so an application needs no OpenBao code. Human login off Tenant members sign in through your OIDC provider; group membership decides access. cert-manager issuance off A cert-manager Issuer per namespace. Cross-tenant trust off Opt-in, directional trust between two tenants' certificate authorities.

Engines exist for every tenant, but grant nothing on their own: a workload gets access only once its ServiceAccount is annotated. Access is never derived from the tenant's accessControl groups (as it is in the Vault integration) — workloads get access from ServiceAccount annotations, people from identity-provider groups named after the tenant.

One OpenBao namespace per tenant, created with the Tenant. The platform namespace holds the certificate authority that signs each tenant's CA. A login to one tenant's namespace gives no access to any other.

docs.title: How tiers map to OpenBao access
docs.text:
A tier is set with bao.stakater.com/tier and applies to every engine the ServiceAccount enables:

Tier Secrets (KV) Encryption (transit) audit-read list names only — no values none viewer read, list none editor create, read, update, patch, list encrypt, decrypt, rewrap admin create, read, update, patch, list, delete the above, plus create, rotate and delete keys

Transit needs write access, so viewer and audit-read get none. Certificates are the exception: a workload that opts into PKI may issue and sign at any tier. For people signing in through OIDC, the tier bounds certificate access as well.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text:
Platform / OpenBao administrator Tenant Sets up once the OpenBao login for the operator; installs the extension — Per tenant nothing annotates ServiceAccounts/Deployments for the access each app needs Never writes per-tenant OpenBao policy by hand holds a static credential, or reaches another tenant's namespace

Built on Template Operator v2

Because the extension renders through Template Operator v2, the permissions it grants are shared with anyone who can author a Template. On a cluster where tenants (or others) can create Templates, read Security → how the extension scopes Template Operator v2 before production.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
1. Installation — prerequisites, the one-time operator bootstrap, install the extension
  2. Giving an application a secret — annotate, write, read from a pod
  3. Secrets and sharing — the KV layout, sharing within and between tenants
  4. Encryption and certificates — transit keys, PKI, cert-manager, cross-tenant trust
  5. Delivery and login — Kubernetes Secrets via External Secrets, and human SSO
  6. Security — the trust boundary and the Template-author caveat
  7. Operating — health, troubleshooting, what deletion does
  8. Reference — the annotation grammar and install values

Next: Installation

docs.title: The annotation grammar
docs.text:
The keys follow one grammar, so you can work out a name instead of looking it up:

  • bao.stakater.com/<engine> — turn an engine on: kv, transit, pki.
  • bao.stakater.com/<engine>-<verb>-<scope> — a sharing grant, always on the ServiceAccount. export and import cross a tenant boundary, subscribe stays inside one tenant. Values are comma-separated lists.
  • bao.stakater.com/<engine>-<request>.<name> — a delivery request, always on the Deployment. <name> becomes the Kubernetes Secret.
  • tier and app carry no engine: they qualify the identity itself.

Grants go on the ServiceAccount, because that is the identity OpenBao authenticates. Requests go on the Deployment, because that is the workload receiving the secret. A key on the wrong object is reported as an error beside the workload rather than ignored.

docs.title: On the ServiceAccount
docs.text: Annotation Engine What it does bao.stakater.com/tier all Required alongside any engine. audit-read, viewer, editor or admin. bao.stakater.com/kv KV "true" — read and write this application's own secrets path. bao.stakater.com/transit Transit "true" — use the application, namespace and tenant encryption keys. bao.stakater.com/pki PKI "true" — issue certificates directly from OpenBao. bao.stakater.com/app KV, Transit Optional. Names the application that owns these secrets; defaults to the ServiceAccount name. bao.stakater.com/kv-subscribe-ns KV Read the shared folders of other namespaces in the same tenant. bao.stakater.com/kv-export-tenant KV Share secrets out to other tenants. bao.stakater.com/kv-import-tenant KV Read secrets other tenants shared in. bao.stakater.com/transit-export-tenant Transit Share an encryption key out to other tenants. bao.stakater.com/transit-import-tenant Transit Use an encryption key another tenant shared in. bao.stakater.com/pki-allow-tenant PKI Accept these tenants as inbound mTLS clients. Implies trusting their CA. bao.stakater.com/pki-trust-tenant PKI Trust these tenants' server certificates when calling them, without accepting them inbound.

docs.title: On the Deployment
docs.text:
Each creates a Kubernetes Secret named <serviceaccount>-<name>:

Annotation Reads from Needs, on the ServiceAccount bao.stakater.com/kv-secret.<name> this application's own path kv bao.stakater.com/kv-subscribe.<name> a sibling namespace's shared folder kv-subscribe-ns bao.stakater.com/kv-import.<name> another tenant's shared space kv-import-tenant

Values take the form <leaf>[#<field>] — with a field, only that field is copied into the Secret; without one, every field becomes a key. The subscribe and import forms are prefixed with the source: team-a-api/postgres and team-a/creds.

docs.title: Install values
docs.text:
Everything under parent is passed to every tenant; values outside it cover the cluster's own setup. See Installation.

Value Default Meaning parent.baoServer — the OpenBao address workloads and ESO use parent.env dev the <env> segment of every secret path parent.eso enabled deliver secrets as Kubernetes Secrets parent.certManager.enabled false a cert-manager Issuer per namespace parent.sso.enabled / .issuerUrl false / "" human login through OIDC parent.pki.roles — the certificate roles tenants issue from (install-wide) platformPki — the CA that signs each tenant's intermediate CA safety — what deletion does

What each tier may do is fixed by the extension and is not a value.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OpenBao Config Operator — the operator that applies this configuration to OpenBao.
  • Tenant — the resource this extension reads.
  • Vault Enterprise extension — the equivalent for HashiCorp Vault Enterprise (KV, sharing, SSO; transit and PKI not supported there yet).

Previous: Operating

docs.title: Secrets and sharing
docs.text:
Each application has its own KV path. Sharing is opt-in on both sides, and the direction is fixed. There are three scopes, and the path tells you which one you are in:

flowchart TB
  subgraph T["team-a/ — the tenant's own OpenBao namespace"]
    A["kv/data/dev/team-a-api/web/<br/><b>private</b> to the web application"]
    B["kv/data/dev/_shared/from-team-a-api/<br/><b>written</b> by team-a-api,<br/><b>read</b> by namespaces that subscribe"]
  end
  subgraph S["shared/ — the cross-tenant namespace"]
    C["kv/data/dev/from-team-a/to-team-b/<br/><b>written</b> by team-a, <b>read</b> by team-b"]
  end

docs.title: Between namespaces in one tenant
docs.text:
Each namespace owns a shared folder that only it can write to; other namespaces in the same tenant subscribe to read it. The folder is named after the writer, so a reader always knows where a value came from.

An editor or admin workload writes to its own folder with no extra annotation — the path is already in its ConfigMap as VAULT_KV_SHARED_OUT_PATH. The reader opts in:

# a ServiceAccount in team-a-worker, reading what team-a-api shared
metadata:
  annotations:
    bao.stakater.com/tier: viewer
    bao.stakater.com/kv-subscribe-ns: team-a-api

Subscribing only ever grants read, so no namespace can write into another namespace's folder. You can only subscribe to namespaces in your own tenant.

docs.title: Between tenants
docs.text:
Cross-tenant secrets live in neither tenant. They go to the shared/ OpenBao namespace, and both sides must opt in:

# a team-a ServiceAccount — may write to team-b
bao.stakater.com/kv-export-tenant: team-b

# a team-b ServiceAccount — may read what team-a sent
bao.stakater.com/kv-import-tenant: team-a

Exporting grants nothing until the other tenant imports, and removing either annotation cuts the link.

Delivering a shared secret

These grants (on the ServiceAccount) open the path. To deliver a shared or imported secret to a workload as a Kubernetes Secret, pair them with the kv-subscribe.<name> / kv-import.<name> request annotations on the Deployment — see Delivery and login.

Previous: Giving an application a secret · Next: Encryption and certificates

docs.title: The trust boundary is the namespace label
docs.text:
The extension finds a tenant's namespaces by the stakater.com/tenant label, and renders a policy and login role for every annotated ServiceAccount in them. So anyone who can set stakater.com/tenant: X on a namespace can give their own ServiceAccounts tenant X's OpenBao access.

Keep the label under the platform's control: only MTO and cluster admins may set or change it, and tenant users must not hold patch/update on namespaces at cluster scope. MTO's own namespace handling relies on the same label.

Inside a tenant, the ServiceAccount annotations decide which app gets which access — anyone who can annotate a ServiceAccount in a tenant namespace can request that tenant's access for it, up to admin. Treat "who can annotate ServiceAccounts in a tenant namespace" as part of the tenant's own trust boundary.

docs.title: How access is scoped
docs.text:
• A workload is confined to one namespace and one application path — the login role is bound to the ServiceAccount, and the policy is scoped to kv/data/<env>/<namespace>/<app>/. Two workloads in one namespace cannot read each other's secrets.
  • Engines grant nothing on their own: an engine annotation without a tier grants nothing, and a ServiceAccount with no bao.stakater.com/* annotation renders nothing.
  • A key on the wrong object (a grant on a Deployment, a request on a ServiceAccount) is reported as an error beside the workload, not silently ignored.
  • Sharing and cross-tenant trust are opt-in on both sides and directional — exporting grants nothing until the peer imports; trusting a peer's certificates does not accept it inbound.
  • People signing in through OIDC get their tier across the tenant; a workload is confined to its namespace. Keep that difference in mind when granting admin.

docs.title: How the extension scopes Template Operator v2
docs.text:
The extension renders through Template Operator v2, which applies objects with its own ServiceAccount. The chart grants that account the permissions this integration needs to manage the resources it renders — the OpenBao Config Operator CRs, the per-workload ConfigMaps and the ExternalSecrets.

Keep one administrative rule: authoring a Template Operator v2 Template is a privileged operation — anyone who can create Templates and TemplateInstances drives the operator with those permissions. MTO's tenant roles do not grant that, and it should not be granted to tenants. Template Operator v2's own security model (the operator applies with its ServiceAccount, scoped by RBAC) is the reference for how those permissions are bounded.

Previous: Delivery and login · Next: Operating

docs.title: Vault Community
docs.text:
Deprecated — Vault Community (v1 – Legacy)

This is the legacy built-in Vault integration, configured through the IntegrationConfig. It is deprecated. The current approach is the Vault Enterprise extension, which renders per-tenant configuration through Template Operator v2. (Vault Enterprise isolates each tenant in its own Vault namespace, which requires Vault Enterprise.)

Vault is an identity-based secret and encryption management system: it validates and authorizes a client — a person, a machine or an application — before giving it access to a secret.

With the Multi-Tenant Operator (MTO), cluster administrators can configure multi-tenancy within their cluster. The Vault integration extends that multi-tenancy into Vault: every tenant gets its own KV secrets engine, along with the policies, identity groups and Kubernetes auth roles that let tenant members and their workloads reach that engine and nothing else.

Note that Vault integration in MTO is optional.

docs.title: What it saves you
docs.text:
Setting a tenant up in Vault by hand means creating, per tenant: a KV secrets engine; an admin policy and a read policy; an identity group for every identity-provider group that should have access, and a group alias on the OIDC accessor for each; and a Kubernetes auth role for every namespace whose workloads need to read secrets. All of it has to be revisited whenever a namespace is added, a team's group membership changes, or a tenant is removed.

MTO derives all of it from the Tenant resource you already maintain, and keeps it in step as the tenant changes — creating what is now needed and removing what no longer applies.

The other half is what it removes from application teams. A developer never writes a Vault policy and never holds a static Vault credential. They add one label to a ServiceAccount, and the pod authenticates with the token Kubernetes already gives it.

flowchart LR
  T["Tenant CR"] --> M["Multi-Tenant Operator"]
  M -->|"KV v2 engine, admin and read policies,<br/>identity group and alias per tenant group"| V[("Vault")]
  M -->|"Kubernetes auth role per namespace<br/>that has a labelled ServiceAccount"| V
  U["Tenant member"] -->|"OIDC login"| V
  S["ServiceAccount<br/>labelled vault-access"] -->|"ServiceAccount token"| V

Per tenant, the only two things written by hand are the Tenant resource and a label on a ServiceAccount. Everything inside Vault is derived from them.

docs.title: What each tenant gets
docs.text:
Capability Default What it is A private KV path on A KV version 2 secrets engine mounted at <tenant>/kv. Tenants cannot see or reach another tenant's path. Human login on Tenant members sign in through the same OIDC identity provider as the cluster, and their IdP group membership places them in a Vault identity group. Workload login on Pods authenticate with their Kubernetes service account token. No static Vault credentials are distributed. A common shared path on One path, commonSecretsPath, shared by every tenant — writable by Owners, readable by Viewers. Editor access off Editors get no Vault access unless a custom policy grants it. Custom policies off The policies block in the IntegrationConfig grants extra access to any tenant role.

MTO keeps all of it in step with the cluster: auth roles are removed when their namespace goes away, identity groups are deleted when they no longer match the tenant's access control, and custom policies are deleted when they are removed from the IntegrationConfig.

docs.title: How tenant roles map to Vault access
docs.text:
Tenant role Policy Vault path Capabilities Owner <tenant>-admin <tenant>/* Create, Read, Update, Delete, List Owner <tenant>-admin sys/mounts/<tenant>/* Create, Read, Update, Delete, List Owner <tenant>-admin <commonSecretsPath>/* Create, Read, Update, Delete, List Viewer <tenant>-read <tenant>/* Read, List Viewer <tenant>-read <commonSecretsPath>/* Read, List Editor — — No access by default

Editors receive Vault access only through a custom policy in the IntegrationConfig whose tenantRoles includes editor. Without one, no Vault identity group is created for the tenant's editor groups.

Workloads get the tenant's <tenant>-read policy, whichever role their namespace's members hold.

docs.title: Setting up the integration
docs.text: These three steps are done once per cluster, by a platform administrator, before any tenant gets a Vault path.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Vault instance reachable from the cluster.
  • The Kubernetes auth method enabled in Vault — workloads always authenticate through it, and so does MTO itself when authMethod is kubernetes.
  • An RHSSO (Red Hat Single Sign-On) instance integrated with Vault over the OIDC login method, for user access.

docs.title: Enabling the integration
docs.text:
Administrators point MTO at Vault by adding the details to the IntegrationConfig:

apiVersion: tenantoperator.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: IntegrationConfig
metadata:
  name: tenant-operator-config
  namespace: multi-tenant-operator
spec:
  integrations:
    vault:
      enabled: true
      authMethod: kubernetes
      accessInfo:
        accessorPath: oidc/
        address: https://vault.apps.prod.abcdefghi.kubeapp.cloud/
        roleName: mto
      config:
        ssoClient: vault
        commonSecretsPath: common-shared-secrets

authMethod accepts kubernetes (the default, shown above) or token. Token authentication uses a secretRef pointing at a secret holding a Vault token, instead of roleName.

accessorPath is the path of the OIDC auth mount in Vault. MTO reads its accessor ID and uses it to alias each tenant group to the identity provider.

commonSecretsPath is a single path shared by all tenants; it defaults to common-shared-secrets when unset. Every field, and the policies block for defining custom tenant policies, is described in the IntegrationConfig documentation.

docs.title: Creating the Vault role for MTO
docs.text:
roleName above names a role under Vault's Kubernetes authentication, which is how MTO reaches Vault. Create that role with a policy granting the following permissions:

path "secret/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "sys/mounts" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}
path "sys/mounts/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "managed-addons/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}
path "auth/kubernetes/role/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "sys/auth" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}
path "sys/policies/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "identity/group" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "identity/group-alias" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "identity/group-alias/id/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "identity/group/name/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}
path "identity/group/id/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "patch", "delete", "list"]
}

docs.title: Giving an application a secret
docs.text: This is the path most people take, and everything else on this page builds on it: create the tenant, write a secret as one of its members, read it from a pod. The examples use tenant bluesky and its namespace bluesky-dev.

docs.title: 1. Create the tenant
docs.text:
Administrators create a tenant as usual. Vault access is granted by group: only the groups entries under accessControl produce Vault access, and users entries do not.

apiVersion: tenantoperator.stakater.com/v1beta3
kind: Tenant
metadata:
  name: bluesky
spec:
  accessControl:
    owners:
      groups:
        - bluesky-owner-group
    viewers:
      groups:
        - bluesky-viewer-group
  quota: small
  namespaces:
    sandboxes:
      enabled: false

MTO then creates, for tenant bluesky:

  • a KV version 2 secrets engine mounted at bluesky/kv;
  • a bluesky-admin policy and a bluesky-read policy;
  • an owner identity group named bluesky, plus one for each group under owners.groups, holding the bluesky-admin policy;
  • an identity group for each group under viewers.groups, holding the bluesky-read policy;
  • a group alias for each of those groups on the OIDC accessor, so a user's IdP group membership places them in the matching Vault group.

docs.title: 2. Write the first secret — user OIDC auth
docs.text:
Someone has to put a secret in. A member of an owner group signs in through OIDC and writes it; their IdP group membership is what carries the bluesky-admin policy.

sequenceDiagram
    participant MTO as Multi-Tenant Operator
    participant Vault
    participant IdP as OIDC provider
    participant User as Tenant member
    MTO->>Vault: create bluesky/kv, bluesky-admin and bluesky-read policies
    MTO->>Vault: create an identity group per tenant group, aliased to the OIDC accessor
    User->>Vault: log in through OIDC
    Vault->>IdP: authenticate and read the group claim
    Vault-->>User: token carrying the group's policy
    User->>Vault: manage secrets under bluesky/kv
vault login -method=oidc
vault kv put bluesky/kv/db-creds username=app password=s3cr3t

docs.title: 3. Label the ServiceAccount — service account auth
docs.text:
MTO enables the Kubernetes auth method, which authenticates a client to Vault with a Kubernetes service account token. For every tenant namespace, MTO creates a Kubernetes auth role named <namespace>-<tenant>-mto, bound to that namespace and carrying the tenant's <tenant>-read policy.

Only service accounts labelled stakater.com/vault-access: true are bound to that role:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: bluesky-app
  namespace: bluesky-dev
  labels:
    stakater.com/vault-access: "true"

Adding or removing the label re-reconciles the namespace. If a namespace has no labelled service account, MTO deletes the role.

sequenceDiagram
    participant MTO as Multi-Tenant Operator
    participant K8s as Kubernetes
    participant Vault
    participant Pod
    MTO->>K8s: watch ServiceAccounts labelled stakater.com/vault-access
    MTO->>Vault: create auth role bluesky-dev-bluesky-mto, policy bluesky-read
    Pod->>Vault: log in with its ServiceAccount token
    Vault->>K8s: verify the token
    Vault-->>Pod: token carrying bluesky-read
    Pod->>Vault: read secrets under bluesky/kv

docs.title: 4. Read the secret from the pod
docs.text:
From a pod running as bluesky-app, exchange the service account token for a Vault token and read the secret written in step 2:

export VAULT_TOKEN=$(vault write -field=token auth/kubernetes/login \
  role=bluesky-dev-bluesky-mto \
  jwt=@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)

vault kv get bluesky/kv/db-creds

The role name is <namespace>-<tenant>-mto, so a pod in bluesky-dev owned by tenant bluesky uses bluesky-dev-bluesky-mto.

Note

Workload access is read-only: the role carries the <tenant>-read policy. Writing secrets to a tenant's path is done by tenant members signed in through OIDC, or by a client using credentials you issue separately.

docs.title: Checking what was created
docs.text:
For tenant bluesky, with a token that can read Vault's configuration:

vault secrets list                                   # bluesky/kv/ is mounted
vault policy read bluesky-admin                      # the owner policy
vault list identity/group/name                       # one group per tenant group
vault read auth/kubernetes/role/bluesky-dev-bluesky-mto

The auth role's bound_service_account_names lists exactly the labelled service accounts in that namespace, and its token_policies holds bluesky-read.

docs.title: When a pod cannot log in
docs.text:
• The auth role only exists while the namespace has at least one service account labelled stakater.com/vault-access: true. The value is the string "true" — quote it in YAML, or Kubernetes rejects the label as a boolean.
  • The role name is <namespace>-<tenant>-mto, not the namespace name.
  • A pod that can read but not write is behaving correctly: workload roles carry <tenant>-read.

docs.title: What deletion does
docs.text:
Warning

Setting enabled: false removes each tenant's <tenant>-admin and <tenant>-read policies and its identity groups, and unmounts its <tenant>/kv secrets engine. Removing that mount deletes the secrets stored in it. Deleting the vault block outright does not run that cleanup — it leaves everything in Vault as it stands.

Deleting a namespace removes its auth role. Removing a group from the tenant's accessControl deletes the matching Vault identity group, so access follows the tenant definition rather than lingering in Vault.

docs.title: Using Microsoft Entra ID group IDs
docs.text:
Vault access follows the groups entries in a tenant's accessControl, matched against the group claim in the token the identity provider issues. Microsoft Entra ID puts group IDs in that claim, not group names — so if your chain is Entra ID behind Keycloak, the tenant must list object IDs, and Keycloak needs two mappers to carry the claim through.

This section applies only to that chain. With an identity provider that emits group names, nothing here is needed.

docs.title: Step 1: Include group IDs in Entra ID tokens
docs.text: In Microsoft Entra ID → App Registrations, open the registration used by Keycloak and configure an optional claim that includes group IDs in the token.

docs.title: Step 2: Import the claim as a user attribute in Keycloak
docs.text:
On the Keycloak identity provider pointing at Entra ID, create an attribute importer mapper:

Setting Value Mapper type User Attribute User attribute groups Claim groups Sync mode FORCE

docs.title: Step 3: Forward the attribute into the Vault client's token
docs.text: On the Vault client in Keycloak, create a protocol mapper that forwards the groups user attribute into the token it issues to Vault.

docs.title: Step 4: Put the group IDs in the tenant
docs.text:
Set the tenant's accessControl groups to the Entra ID object IDs rather than group names:

apiVersion: tenantoperator.stakater.com/v1beta3
kind: Tenant
metadata:
  name: arsenal
spec:
  accessControl:
    owners:
      groups:
        - <object-id>

MTO creates the Vault identity group and its alias from whatever string is listed there, so once the object IDs match the claim, a member of that Entra ID group signing in through OIDC lands in the tenant's Vault group.

docs.title: Delivery and login
docs.text: Two ways people and workloads reach the secrets: External Secrets delivers them to workloads as Kubernetes Secrets, and human SSO lets tenant members sign in to the Vault UI.

docs.title: Delivering secrets with External Secrets
docs.text:
With parent.eso enabled (the default), a workload gets its secret as an ordinary Kubernetes Secret — no Vault code in the app. Annotate the Deployment; its serviceAccountName must be a ServiceAccount already annotated for Vault access (Giving an application a secret).

Annotation Value Reads vault.stakater.com/kv-secret.<name> <leaf>[#<key>] the app's own <leaf> vault.stakater.com/kv-subscribe.<name> <writer-ns>/<leaf>[#<key>] a subscribed _shared/ leaf vault.stakater.com/kv-import.<name> <peer>/<leaf>[#<key>] an imported cross-tenant leaf 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: acme-shop
  annotations:
    vault.stakater.com/kv-secret.db: db-creds          # whole leaf -> Secret
    vault.stakater.com/kv-secret.token: api#token       # one key of a leaf
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: checkout

Each annotation renders an ExternalSecret and a Secret named <serviceaccount>-<name> (here checkout-db, checkout-token), which the pod consumes with envFrom/secretKeyRef as usual. A Deployment whose ServiceAccount does not grant the path gets a vault-config-<deployment>.deploy-error ConfigMap explaining why.

Tip

A rotated value in Vault flows to the Secret on the next ESO refresh. Pair it with Reloader to roll the pods automatically.

docs.title: Human SSO
docs.text:
parent.sso.enabled=true with parent.sso.issuerUrl gives each tenant an OIDC mount oidc/sso and one Vault role per entry of sso.roles, bound to the identity-provider group <tenant>-<role>s (configurable with sso.tenantGroupTemplate). A member logs in to the tenant's Vault namespace and gets exactly the role their group grants — the same roles as workloads (viewer, editor, admin, audit-read):

VAULT_NAMESPACE=<vco.namespace>/acme \
  vault login -method=oidc -path=oidc/sso role=sso.acme.editor

All tenants share one identity-provider client, tenantValues.sso.oidc.clientId (default vault); set it to the ID of Vault's client in your IdP. parent.sso.issuerUrl is the issuer Vault talks to (Dex's, when Keycloak sits behind Dex). The client secret is a Secret vault-oidc-client-secret (key client-secret) in configNamespace.

A login refused for the group is not a 403 — Vault answers "does not match any associated bound claim values", so a user outside the tenant's groups simply cannot sign in to that namespace.

Previous: Secrets and sharing · Next: Security

docs.title: Giving an application a secret
docs.text: This is the day-to-day workflow — written from the developer's hands. It assumes the extension is installed (Installation) and the tenant acme has a labelled namespace acme-shop.

docs.title: 1. Annotate the ServiceAccount
docs.text:
Give the app its own KV prefix and an access role:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: acme-shop
  annotations:
    vault.stakater.com/kv: "true"
    vault.stakater.com/role: editor      # read + write (see Overview → roles)

The extension renders, in the tenant's Vault namespace, a Policy and a Kubernetes login role named kv.acme.acme-shop.checkout, and a ConfigMap vault-config-checkout in acme-shop holding the VAULT_* values the app needs:

VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_NAMESPACE=<vco.namespace>/acme, VAULT_K8S_MOUNT=kubernetes/workloads,
VAULT_K8S_ROLE=kv.acme.acme-shop.checkout, VAULT_KV_APP_PATH=kv/data/dev/acme-shop/checkout

A wrongly configured annotation produces a vault-config-checkout.error ConfigMap explaining what is wrong, and nothing else — one app's mistake never breaks the tenant's other apps.

docs.title: 2. Read and write from the pod
docs.text:
The pod logs in with its ServiceAccount token (which Kubernetes mounts at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token) and uses the values from the ConfigMap:

# values come from the vault-config-checkout ConfigMap, mounted as env
export VAULT_ADDR VAULT_NAMESPACE
TOKEN=$(vault write -field=token auth/"$VAULT_K8S_MOUNT"/login \
  role="$VAULT_K8S_ROLE" \
  jwt=@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)

VAULT_TOKEN=$TOKEN vault kv put  -mount=kv "$VAULT_KV_APP_PATH" db-password=s3cret
VAULT_TOKEN=$TOKEN vault kv get  -mount=kv "$VAULT_KV_APP_PATH"

An editor can write; a viewer can only read; an audit-read can list names but not read values. Nothing the app does can reach another app's path, another namespace, or another tenant.

Prefer delivery over in-app Vault calls

Most apps should not call Vault at all. Annotate the Deployment instead and the secret arrives as an ordinary Kubernetes Secret through External Secrets — see Delivery and login. Use the in-pod calls above only when an app genuinely needs the Vault API.

docs.title: 3. Mount the config into the Deployment
docs.text:
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: checkout       # the annotated ServiceAccount
      containers:
        - name: checkout
          image: acme/checkout:1.0
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: vault-config-checkout

docs.title: What an application cannot do
docs.text:
• Read or write outside its own kv/data/<env>/<namespace>/<app>/ prefix (unless sharing is set up — see Secrets and sharing).
  • Reach another tenant's Vault namespace — login is bound to the tenant's namespace and the app's ServiceAccount.
  • Exceed its role — a viewer cannot write, an editor cannot destroy versions.
  • Use an unknown vault.stakater.com/ annotation — it is rejected with an error ConfigMap, not ignored.

Previous: Installation · Next: Secrets and sharing

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: For a platform administrator: a Vault admin sets up the login VCO uses once, then you install the bootstrap chart once. There is no per-tenant installation step.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Vault Enterprise (tested on 2.1.1). Tenant isolation is one Vault namespace per tenant, and namespaces exist only in Enterprise. On Community Edition every tenant's objects land in root and collide. vault-config-operator (VCO) v1.0.3 or later — the first release with spec.authentication.targetNamespace and the Namespace fix the charts rely on. Template Operator v2 (templates.v2.stakater.com) Required — the extension is configuration for it and does nothing without it. 0.0.8 recommended. Multi-Tenant Operator the Tenant CRD. MTO labels each tenant namespace stakater.com/tenant: <tenant>; that label is what the charts key on. External Secrets Operator only if parent.eso is enabled (the default) — see Delivery and login.

docs.title: Install Template Operator v2
docs.text: The simplest route is to let MTO deploy it: set components.templateOperatorV2.mode: Managed in the IntegrationConfig. MTO then runs it in multi-tenant-operator as the ServiceAccount tenant-operator-template-operator-v2 — the value used for templateOperator below. To install it yourself from its chart instead, it runs as template-operator-v2 in stakater-template-operator.

docs.title: Install vault-config-operator
docs.text:
The extension renders vault-config-operator (VCO) custom resources, so VCO must be running on the cluster — v1.0.3 or later (see Requirements). Install it from OperatorHub or with its Helm chart, following the operator's own README. The Vault bootstrap below then sets up the Kubernetes-auth login VCO uses.

VCO logs in to Vault with the Kubernetes auth method once, in vco.namespace (empty = root), as the ServiceAccount the bootstrap chart creates. Before the chart can do anything, a Vault admin sets up that login:

vault auth enable kubernetes
vault write auth/kubernetes/config kubernetes_host=https://kubernetes.default.svc:443
vault policy write vco-admin examples/vco-admin-policy.hcl
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/vco-admin \
  bound_service_account_names=vco-admin \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=vault-config \
  token_policies=vco-admin token_ttl=1h

examples/vco-admin-policy.hcl (in the repo) is the production policy — it denies delete on the data-bearing paths, which is the protection described in Operating → deletion. kubernetes_host without token_reviewer_jwt means Vault reviews tokens with its own ServiceAccount (bound to system:auth-delegator, as the HashiCorp chart does by default), so no reviewer credential is stored.

The policy grants child namespaces with a +

The policy lives in the login namespace and reaches a tenant namespace by prefixing paths with a + segment (e.g. +/sys/policy/*). That follows from how Vault matches a policy path against the full request path including the namespace.

docs.title: Install the bootstrap chart
docs.text:
helm upgrade --install mto-extension-vault-enterprise-bootstrap \
  oci://ghcr.io/stakater/public/charts/mto-extension-vault-enterprise-bootstrap \
  --namespace vault-config --create-namespace \
  --set parent.vaultServer=https://vault.example.com:8200 \
  --set templateOperator.serviceAccountName=tenant-operator-template-operator-v2 \
  --set templateOperator.namespace=multi-tenant-operator

The ServiceAccount must be your Template Operator v2's

The RBAC the chart installs binds to templateOperator. If it names an account that is not the one Template Operator v2 runs as, helm install still succeeds but nothing reconciles — the parent cannot list Tenants. The values above are for an MTO-managed Template Operator v2; a standalone install uses template-operator-v2 in stakater-template-operator.

Key bootstrap values — full list in Reference:

Value Default Meaning configNamespace vault-config holds every Template, TemplateInstance and VCO CR; install the chart here vco.namespace "" (root) the Vault namespace VCO logs in to, and the parent of every tenant namespace parent.vaultServer — the Vault address workloads and ESO use parent.eso enabled "enabled" / "disabled" — a string, not a boolean tenantValues {} any other tenant-chart value, install-wide (CA bundle, monitoring, SSO, …)

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n vault-config get templateinstances.templates.v2.stakater.com \
  -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,READY:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status'

A row per tenant (plus the parent) with READY=True. Then confirm the Vault namespaces exist (vault namespace list), one per tenant.

Tip

Always use the fully-qualified templateinstances.templates.v2.stakater.com. On OpenShift a bare kubectl get templateinstance returns OpenShift's own kind with an empty status — indistinguishable from "nothing is reconciling".

Previous: Overview · Next: Giving an application a secret

docs.title: Operating
docs.text: Day-2 for a platform administrator: how to read health, what to check when a workload cannot log in, what deletion does, and how to uninstall safely.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
A child TemplateInstance being Ready means its VCO resources were applied, not that VCO could write them to Vault. Each child's status.outputs carries two fields per VCO kind, keyed by object name:

Field Meaning <kind>Succeeded ["True"] once VCO has written the object at least once; [] means never — the one unambiguous failure <kind>LastError the message of the most recent failed reconcile, ever — it stays after the object recovers

VCO status cannot say 'healthy now'

VCO sets ReconcileSuccessful and ReconcileFailed side by side and both timestamps freeze after the first write, so there is no live health bit. The .eso TemplateInstance's ExternalSecret outputs are the signal that tracks the data path now; and see Monitoring.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
A workload cannot log in. In order:

  • Its ServiceAccount is not annotated, or has a rejected annotation — look for a vault-config-<sa>.error ConfigMap in the workload namespace.
  • Its namespace is not labelled stakater.com/tenant: <tenant>, so the parent does not see it.
  • The tenant was skipped (name not a DNS label, longer than 63 chars, or equal to the shared-namespace name) — check the skipped-tenants ConfigMap in configNamespace.

Nothing reconciles for any tenant. The parent cannot read its inputs — almost always templateOperator not matching Template Operator v2's real identity, or a missing CRD/version mismatch. Read the parent TemplateInstance's conditions in configNamespace.

An object shows <kind>Succeeded: []. VCO could not write it; read <kind>LastError for the cause (often a Vault permission or a Community-Edition cluster).

docs.title: Deletion
docs.text:
VCO has no deletion policy: when a CR is deleted, VCO deletes the object in Vault. For a Namespace CR that deletes the tenant's Vault namespace and every secret in it, which Vault cannot restore.

The protection is the VCO login's Vault policy: do not grant delete on sys/namespaces/* or the tenants' sys/mounts/* (the production examples/vco-admin-policy.hcl does not). the delete then fails, the data stays, and the CR sits in Terminating with the VCO finalizer until a person decides. To really delete a tenant, a Vault admin deletes the namespace, then removes the finalizer.

A tenant's Vault namespace and KV mount are rendered by the parent, so they live as long as the Tenant — deleting a tenant's last namespace removes its grants but keeps its secrets, and labelling a namespace again brings the grants back. A cross-tenant share lives in the shared namespace, so deleting a tenant never deletes it.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: tenantValues.monitoring.enabled=true gives each tenant a PrometheusRule with one alert, VaultExternalSecretSyncFailed: an ExternalSecret in one of the tenant's namespaces has Ready=False for 5 minutes. It needs the ESO metrics scraped. There is no alert on the VCO objects — their status cannot carry one (see Health).

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
Order matters. Delete the parent TemplateInstance first, wait until every VCO CR is gone, and only then uninstall the release:

kubectl -n vault-config delete templateinstances.templates.v2.stakater.com \
  mto-extension-vault-enterprise-parent --wait
kubectl -n vault-config get namespaces.redhatcop.redhat.io,policies.redhatcop.redhat.io   # wait for "No resources"
helm uninstall mto-extension-vault-enterprise-bootstrap -n vault-config

A plain helm uninstall first would delete the RBAC and the VCO login ServiceAccount in the same step as the parent, leaving every CR stuck in Terminating. With the delete-denying Vault policy, the data-bearing CRs stay Terminating in either order — that is the intended protection, not a failure. Use the full resource name: on OpenShift the short name is OpenShift's own template.openshift.io kind.

Previous: Security · Next: Reference

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Give every tenant its own Vault Enterprise namespace — with a KV secrets engine, Kubernetes login, per-application policies and (optionally) human SSO and delivery as Kubernetes Secrets — derived from the Tenant you already maintain and kept in sync as it changes.

Note

This is the Helm-chart Vault Enterprise extension (mto-extension-vault-enterprise). It is separate from the deprecated Vault Community integration; use this one for per-tenant Vault Enterprise namespaces.

Requires Template Operator v2, VCO and Vault Enterprise

The extension is configuration — it installs no controller of its own. It renders Template Operator v2 objects (templates.v2.stakater.com), which in turn render vault-config-operator (VCO) custom resources; VCO writes them to Vault. Both operators must be running, and Vault must be Enterprise (tenant isolation is one Vault namespace per tenant, and namespaces exist only in Enterprise). See Installation.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
You maintain The extension keeps in sync a Tenant a Vault namespace per tenant, with its own kv/ mount namespaces labelled for it a Kubernetes auth mount workloads log in with a ServiceAccount annotation per app a policy + login role per app, scoped to its own KV path (optional) a Deployment annotation the secret delivered as a Kubernetes Secret via External Secrets

You write — annotate a workload's ServiceAccount:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: acme-shop            # a namespace labelled stakater.com/tenant: acme
  annotations:
    vault.stakater.com/kv: "true"      # give this app its own KV prefix
    vault.stakater.com/role: editor    # read + write there

You get — inside the tenant's Vault namespace, created for you:

  • a KV path the app can reach, kv/data/<env>/acme-shop/checkout/…,
  • a Vault Policy and a Kubernetes login role kv.acme.acme-shop.checkout,
  • a ConfigMap vault-config-checkout in acme-shop with the VAULT_* values the app needs to log in and find its path.

The pod logs in with the ServiceAccount token Kubernetes already gives it — no static Vault credential.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    T[Tenants] --> P[parent TemplateInstance]
    N[Namespaces] --> P
    P -- per tenant --> NS["Vault namespace<br/>+ kv mount"]
    P -- per tenant with a labelled ns --> C["child TemplateInstance<br/>(tenant chart)"]
    C -- renders --> VCO["vault-config-operator CRs"]
    VCO -- writes --> V[Vault Enterprise]

A bootstrap chart (installed once) runs the parent, which renders each tenant's Vault namespace and KV mount itself and emits one child TemplateInstance per tenant that has a labelled namespace. Each child pulls the tenant chart and renders that tenant's VCO resources. The tenant's Vault namespace and KV mount are rendered by the parent, so they live as long as the Tenant — not as long as its namespaces.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text: Platform / Vault administrator Tenant Sets up once the Vault login for VCO; installs the bootstrap chart — Per tenant nothing annotates ServiceAccounts/Deployments for the access each app needs Never writes per-tenant Vault policies by hand holds a static Vault credential, or reaches another tenant's namespace

docs.title: How roles map to Vault access
docs.text:
A workload's vault.stakater.com/role sets what it may do on its KV paths:

Role KV capabilities audit-read list names only — no values viewer read, list editor create, read, update, patch, list admin editor, plus delete and destroy versions

Human SSO users get the same roles, from their identity-provider group — see Delivery and login.

Built on Template Operator v2

Because the extension renders through Template Operator v2, the permissions the bootstrap grants are shared with anyone who can author a Template. On a cluster where tenants (or others) can create Templates, read Security → how the extension scopes Template Operator v2 before production.
