This permits shared-platform plus every namespace labelled kind=tenant.

docs.title: When a namespace is not permitted
docs.text:
The TemplateInstance reconcile sets:

status:
  phase: Failed
  conditions:
    - type: TargetNamespaceAllowed
      status: "False"
      reason: NamespaceNotPermitted
      message: |
        Namespace team-x is not permitted to instantiate Template provider/foo-template.
        Check Template's targetNamespaces configuration
    - type: Ready
      status: "False"
      reason: NamespaceNotPermitted

The operator retries a refused instance after an increasing delay, and also reconciles it when the Template or the TemplateInstance changes. A label change on the consumer namespace does not trigger a reconcile by itself, and an instance that is already applied is not checked again until it reconciles (under sync.mode: off it is frozen). To resolve, either widen the Template's policy to include the consumer namespace, or move the TemplateInstance to a namespace the policy already permits.

docs.title: RBAC required
docs.text: The operator's service account needs get on Namespace to read consumer-namespace labels for selector mode. This is pre-granted by the chart.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Target namespaces for examples.
  • API reference: TargetNamespaces.

docs.title: Composing TemplateInstances
docs.text: A Template can render TemplateInstances — a parent that fans out to one child instance per item, where each child renders the real resources. This is the pattern platform integrations are built on: it gives every item its own status, isolates failures, and keeps the watch count flat.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
Rendering to many namespaces emits the target resources directly from one instance. Prefer composition instead when you want, per item:

  • its own status — each child TemplateInstance reports its own conditions, so you can see which item failed;
  • failure isolation — a malformed render for one item fails only that child, not the whole fan-out;
  • a bounded, shared watch — the parent holds one cluster-wide watch regardless of how many children it emits.

docs.title: The two Templates
docs.text:
The child renders the actual resource for one item, from parameters:

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: namespace-quota-child
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: namespace
      required: true
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: default-quota
      namespace: {{ .parameters.namespace }}
    spec:
      hard:
        pods: "20"
  sync:
    mode: strict

The parent lists namespaces and emits one child TemplateInstance per match. Child instances live in the provider namespace; the child Template's default targetNamespaces (its own namespace) already allows that.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: namespace-quota-parent
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: namespaces
      required: true
  gotemplate: |
    {{- range $ns := .parameters.namespaces }}
    {{- if and (hasKey (default dict (index $ns.metadata "labels")) "team") (not (hasKey $ns.metadata "deletionTimestamp")) }}
    ---
    apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
    kind: TemplateInstance
    metadata:
      name: quota-{{ $ns.metadata.name }}
      namespace: provider
    spec:
      templateRef:
        name: namespace-quota-child
        namespace: provider
      parameters:
        - name: namespace
          value: {{ $ns.metadata.name | quote }}
    {{- end }}
    {{- end }}
  outputs:
    - name: children
      fromAll:
        apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
        kind: TemplateInstance
        namespace: provider
      keyTemplate: "{.metadata.name}"
      fields:
        - name: ready
          jsonPath: "{.status.conditions[?(@.type=='Ready')].status}"
  sync:
    mode: revert

Bind the parent with a LIST of namespaces, exactly as in the fan-out guide. The operator creates a child TemplateInstance per team namespace, each of which renders its ResourceQuota. The deletionTimestamp check drops the child when its namespace is being deleted; without it, the strict child would block the namespace deletion.

docs.title: One place to read health
docs.text:
The parent's outputs aggregate every child's Ready condition, so a single object answers "is every item reconciled?":

kubectl get templateinstance namespace-quota-parent -n provider \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.outputs.ready}' | jq .
# { "quota-team-a": "[\"True\"]", "quota-team-b": "[\"True\"]" }

The [?(...)] filter is a list query, so each value is a JSON-encoded list.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: A child's name is composed from the item (quota-<namespace>). Choose a prefix the parent's own name can never take, so a crafted item value cannot produce a child that collides with the parent instance.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Rendering to many namespaces — the simpler, direct fan-out.
  • Outputs — aggregating child status with fromAll.
  • Lifecycle — how the operator cleans up children when the parent stops emitting them.

docs.title: Deploying Helm Charts
docs.text: Examples of using a Helm chart as a Template's body. For the chart-source rules, Helm SDK selection, valuesTemplate, release-name semantics, and validation behavior, see Helm. For private repositories, see Deploying private Helm charts.

docs.title: Scenario 1: public HTTPS repository
docs.text:
Bill publishes the upstream nginx chart from Bitnami, parameterized so each consumer can pick a replica count.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: nginx-template
  namespace: provider
spec:
  helm:
    version: v4   # the default v3 SDK renders this chart's PodDisruptionBudget with the removed policy/v1beta1 API
    chart:
      repository:
        url: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
        name: nginx
        version: 18.1.0
    releaseName: nginx
    valuesTemplate: |
      replicaCount: {{ .parameters.replicas }}
      image:
        repository: bitnamilegacy/nginx   # Bitnami moved its versioned images here
      service:
        type: ClusterIP
  parameters:
    - name: replicas
      value: "2"
  targetNamespaces:
    explicit:
      allow:
        literal:
          - team-a

A consuming TemplateInstance:

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: nginx
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: nginx-template
    namespace: provider
  parameters:
    - name: replicas
      value: "3"

docs.title: Scenario 2: OCI registry
docs.text:
OCI-hosted charts use the oci:// scheme. Everything else is identical to the HTTPS case:

spec:
  helm:
    chart:
      repository:
        url: oci://ghcr.io/stakater/charts
        name: my-chart
        version: 0.1.0

docs.title: Scenario 3: driving values from instance metadata
docs.text:
valuesTemplate is a Go template, so the consuming TemplateInstance's name, namespace, and labels are available alongside parameters:

spec:
  helm:
    chart:
      repository:
        url: https://charts.example.com
        name: app
        version: 1.0.0
    valuesTemplate: |
      ingress:
        enabled: true
        hosts:
          - host: {{ .instance.name }}.example.com
            paths:
              - path: /
                pathType: Prefix
      resources:
        limits:
          cpu: {{ .parameters.cpuLimit }}
          memory: {{ .parameters.memLimit }}
  parameters:
    - name: cpuLimit
      value: "500m"
    - name: memLimit
      value: "256Mi"

Each TemplateInstance automatically gets an ingress host derived from its own name.

docs.title: Repository URL rules
docs.text:
• spec.helm.chart.repository.url must match the pattern ^(https?|oci)://.
  • version must follow SemVer 2, e.g. 1.2.3, 1.2.3-rc.1+meta. Ranges, latest, and floating versions are rejected at admission time. Write the version without a v prefix: the API accepts v1.2.3, but the chart then fails to load.

docs.title: Status on failure
docs.text:
If the chart cannot be pulled, the Template reports:

status:
  phase: Error
  conditions:
    - type: SourceAccessible
      status: "False"
      reason: RepositoryUnreachable
      message: "source access failed: failed to pull chart..."

The reconcile is retried after 60 seconds, so transient registry outages self-heal. See Helm for the full set of conditions and reasons set during validation.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Helm for the model, SDK selection, and valuesTemplate rendering.
  • Deploying private Helm charts for auth Secrets and registry tokens.
  • API reference: HelmSpec.

docs.title: Deploying Private Helm Charts
docs.text:
A Template can pull from a private Helm repository, either an HTTP/HTTPS repo with basic auth, or an OCI registry with basic auth or a Docker config.

Authentication is configured by referencing a Secret from spec.helm.chart.repository.auth.secretRef. The Secret must live in the same namespace as the Template (the provider namespace), not the consumer namespace.

docs.title: Supported credential layouts
docs.text:
The operator reads the following keys from the referenced Secret:

Source type Keys Behavior HTTP(S) repository username, password Sent as HTTP Basic auth on chart pull. OCI registry username, password Sent as HTTP Basic auth to the registry. OCI registry .dockerconfigjson A standard Kubernetes kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson secret. The operator writes it to a temp file and passes it to the OCI client.

If both username/password and .dockerconfigjson are present in the same secret, username/password win.

Token-based authentication

For registries that authenticate with a personal access token, robot token, or API key (GitHub Container Registry, GitLab, Harbor, and similar), place the token in the password field of the Secret. Set username to whatever value the registry expects, typically your account name or a registry-specific placeholder such as token or oauth2. The operator passes both fields to Helm as HTTP Basic auth; the registry decides how to interpret them.

docs.title: Private HTTPS repository
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: nexus-creds
  namespace: provider
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: ci-user
  password: <token-or-password>
---
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: private-chart
  namespace: provider
spec:
  helm:
    chart:
      repository:
        url: https://nexus.example.com/repository/helm
        name: my-chart
        version: 1.4.0
        auth:
          secretRef:
            name: nexus-creds
    releaseName: my-chart

docs.title: Private OCI registry: basic auth
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: ghcr-creds
  namespace: provider
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: ghcr-user
  password: <pat>
---
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: oci-private
  namespace: provider
spec:
  helm:
    chart:
      repository:
        url: oci://ghcr.io/stakater/charts
        name: my-chart
        version: 0.1.0
        auth:
          secretRef:
            name: ghcr-creds

docs.title: Private OCI registry: Docker config
docs.text:
If you already have a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson pull secret, point at it directly:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: ghcr-dockerconfig
  namespace: provider
type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
data:
  .dockerconfigjson: <base64-encoded-config>
---
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: oci-private-dockerconfig
  namespace: provider
spec:
  helm:
    chart:
      repository:
        url: oci://ghcr.io/stakater/charts
        name: my-chart
        version: 0.1.0
        auth:
          secretRef:
            name: ghcr-dockerconfig

docs.title: Credentials stay with the provider
docs.text: The Secret lives where the Template lives. This keeps registry credentials out of consumer namespaces and gives the platform team full control over chart access. RBAC on the provider namespace is the boundary that protects the credentials.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
If the secret is missing, malformed, or the credentials are wrong, the operator reports:

status:
  phase: Error
  conditions:
    - type: SourceAccessible
      status: "False"
      reason: RepositoryUnreachable
      message: "source access failed: failed to pull chart ... unauthorized"

The reconcile is retried after 60 seconds, so rotating credentials in-place is non-disruptive.

docs.title: Deploying a Template
docs.text: This guide walks through the basic flow: a platform team creates a Template in a provider namespace, and a consumer team creates a TemplateInstance in their own namespace to render it.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Bill is a platform admin who wants to publish a reusable Pod blueprint. Anna leads team A and wants to use that blueprint, with her own values, in team-a.

docs.title: 1. Bill creates the namespaces and the Template
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: foo
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: foo-template
  namespace: foo
spec:
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: {{ .parameters.name }}
      namespace: {{ .instance.namespace }}
      labels:
        app: {{ .parameters.name }}
        managed-by: template-operator
    spec:
      restartPolicy: {{ .parameters.restartPolicy }}
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: {{ .parameters.image }}
          env:
            - name: ENDPOINT
              value: {{ .parameters.endpoint }}
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
  parameters:
    - name: name
      value: example
    - name: image
      value: nginx:latest
    - name: endpoint
      value: http://default-endpoint
    - name: restartPolicy
      value: Always
  targetNamespaces:
    explicit:
      allow:
        literal:
          - team-a

Apply it:

kubectl apply -f template.yaml

Confirm the Template validated:

kubectl -n foo get template foo-template -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'

Expected output:

Valid

docs.title: 2. Anna creates a TemplateInstance
docs.text:
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: foo-template
    namespace: foo
  parameters:
    - name: name
      value: my-custom-pod
    - name: image
      value: nginx:1.27
    - name: endpoint
      value: http://api.team-a.svc
    - name: restartPolicy
      value: OnFailure

kubectl apply -f templateinstance.yaml

Confirm the instance is Ready:

kubectl -n team-a get templateinstance my-app

Expected output:

NAME     PHASE
my-app   Ready

The rendered Pod is now in team-a:

kubectl -n team-a get pod my-custom-pod

docs.title: 3. Inspect what was rendered
docs.text:
status.renderedResources lists the resources the operator owns for this instance:

kubectl -n team-a get templateinstance my-app -o yaml

status:
  phase: Ready
  resolvedTemplateRef:
    name: foo-template
    namespace: foo
    generation: 1
  resolvedParameters:
    - name: name
    - name: image
    - name: endpoint
    - name: restartPolicy
  renderedResources:
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      name: my-custom-pod
      namespace: team-a
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      reason: Reconciled

docs.title: 4. Updating
docs.text:
With sync.mode: revert or strict, editing the TemplateInstance's parameters re-renders, and editing the Template re-renders every TemplateInstance that references it. In both cases, resources that were rendered before but not after are deleted.

This Template uses the default sync.mode: off, so after the first clean apply the instance is frozen and neither edit is applied. See Sync.

docs.title: 5. Deleting
docs.text:
kubectl -n team-a delete templateinstance my-app

Every resource in status.renderedResources is deleted, the operator's finalizer is stripped, then the TemplateInstance's own finalizer is removed.

To delete the Template, first delete every TemplateInstance that references it. Otherwise the deletion is held with Deleting=False, Reason=DeletionBlocked.

docs.title: Distributing a ConfigMap
docs.text: A TemplateInstance can read one resource and copy it into many — and because the source is watched, every copy updates when the source changes. The worked example is a CA bundle distributed to every workload namespace, but the mechanism suits any cluster-wide value.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Bill maintains a CA bundle in a ConfigMap ca-bundle in the provider namespace, and wants a read-only copy named trusted-ca in every namespace labelled team. Rotating the bundle should update every copy.

docs.title: The Template
docs.text:
Two parameters: the source (GET mode — a named objectFieldRef) and the target namespaces (LIST mode). Both are watched, so a change to either re-renders.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: distribute-ca
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: caBundle
      required: true
    - name: namespaces
      required: true
  gotemplate: |
    {{- range $ns := .parameters.namespaces }}
    {{- if and (hasKey (default dict (index $ns.metadata "labels")) "team") (not (hasKey $ns.metadata "deletionTimestamp")) }}
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: trusted-ca
      namespace: {{ $ns.metadata.name }}
    data:
      ca.crt: {{ $.parameters.caBundle | quote }}
    {{- end }}
    {{- end }}
  sync:
    mode: revert     # a hand-edit of a copy converges back to the source

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: distribute-ca
  namespace: provider
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: distribute-ca
    namespace: provider
  parameters:
    - name: caBundle
      valueFrom:
        objectFieldRef:
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: ConfigMap
          name: ca-bundle            # named -> GET mode
          namespace: provider
          jsonPath: .data.ca\.crt
    - name: namespaces
      valueFrom:
        objectFieldRef:
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Namespace
          jsonPath: .items

Inside range, . is the current namespace, so the template reads the bundle through $.parameters. The deletionTimestamp check skips a namespace that is being deleted, so that namespace can finish its deletion.

Update ca-bundle and every trusted-ca copy is re-rendered on the next reconcile.

Don't copy Secret material into ConfigMaps

This copies a public CA bundle. Never read a Secret and render its contents into a ConfigMap (or into status — see outputs); that exposes it. For private key material, deliver it where it is needed with a dedicated mechanism rather than fanning it out. A Secret is also refused as an output source.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Rendering to many namespaces for the fan-out half of this pattern.
  • Parameters: objectFieldRef GET vs LIST and valueFrom.secretKeyRef for reading secret values safely at render time.

docs.title: Drift Protection
docs.text:
Examples of configuring Template.spec.sync to control drift on rendered resources. For the three modes, the comparison rules, and what each one does internally, see Sync.

Cert-manager prerequisite

sync.mode: strict requires cert-manager to be installed on the cluster, since the operator's validating webhook needs TLS. The Helm chart provisions a self-signed Issuer and a Certificate, but it does not install cert-manager itself.

docs.title: Scenario 1: enforce a baseline NetworkPolicy (strict)
docs.text:
Bill wants to publish a NetworkPolicy that consumers cannot edit or delete by hand. Strict mode rejects unauthorized edits at the API server.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: tenant-network-policy
  namespace: provider
spec:
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: deny-cross-tenant
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      policyTypes: [Ingress]
      ingress:
        - from:
            - namespaceSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  kind: tenant
  sync:
    mode: strict

An attempt by a consumer to kubectl edit the rendered NetworkPolicy is rejected by the admission webhook with a message that points back at the owning TemplateInstance. The operator's own reconciles pass through unhindered.

docs.title: Scenario 2: keep a Deployment in sync but let HPA scale it (revert + ignoreFields)
docs.text:
Bill publishes a Deployment and wants the rendered shape preserved on every reconcile, but Anna runs a HorizontalPodAutoscaler against it. Strict mode would block HPA's updates to spec.replicas. Revert mode plus ignoreFields is the right tool.

spec:
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    ...
  sync:
    mode: revert
    ignoreFields:
      - spec.replicas
      - metadata.annotations

The controller reverts any drift in the rest of the Deployment spec on the next reconcile, but leaves spec.replicas and metadata.annotations to whoever last wrote them.

docs.title: Scenario 3: bootstrap a resource that another controller will own (off)
docs.text:
Bill publishes a Certificate for cert-manager to rotate. After cert-manager picks it up, it rewrites the associated Secret's data field on rotation. The default sync.mode: off is what Bill wants:

spec:
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
    kind: Certificate
    ...
  # sync omitted -> mode defaults to off

Resources are applied once and then left alone: after the first clean apply the instance freezes, and neither Template nor TemplateInstance changes re-apply anything (see Sync).

docs.title: Verifying that sync is active
docs.text:
When sync.mode is revert or strict, the TemplateInstance reports a Synced condition:

status:
  conditions:
    - type: Synced
      status: "True"
      reason: SyncActive

The Ready condition continues to reflect overall reconciliation success.

docs.title: Disabling sync without unbinding resources
docs.text: Changing Template.spec.sync.mode back to off (or removing spec.sync entirely) releases the drift watches on the next reconcile. The rendered resources stay in place; they are no longer enforced.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Sync for the model, the three modes, and how the webhook works in strict mode.
  • API reference: SyncConfig.

docs.title: Orphan Resource Handling
docs.text: Examples of how the operator handles resources that were rendered last time but not this time. For the cleanup model, ownership metadata, and how failed cleanups are retried, see Lifecycle.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Bill shrinks a Template
docs.text:
Bill's Template originally renders a Deployment, a Service, and a ConfigMap. Anna's TemplateInstance has applied all three to team-a.

Bill updates the Template to drop the ConfigMap. With sync.mode: revert or strict, on the next reconcile of Anna's TemplateInstance, the operator applies the two surviving resources and deletes the now-orphaned ConfigMap. Anna does not have to do anything.

Under the default sync.mode: off, the instance is frozen after its first clean apply, so the ConfigMap stays until the mode changes.

docs.title: Scenario 2: a bad Template update is rejected without losing resources
docs.text:
If Bill ships a Template update whose new render is invalid (broken manifest, unknown CRD, schema error), the operator detects the problem before applying anything. The previously-rendered resources stay in place untouched, and the TemplateInstance reports Phase=Failed with a condition explaining the issue.

Once Bill fixes the Template, the next reconcile applies the corrected output and cleans up any orphans normally.

docs.title: Scenario 3: Anna sees a Failed cleanup in status
docs.text:
If the operator can't delete an orphan, for example because another controller's webhook blocks the delete, the orphan is retained in status.renderedResources with status: Failed:

status:
  phase: Failed
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "False"
      reason: DisposalFailed
  renderedResources:
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: ConfigMap
      name: leftover-config
      namespace: team-a
      status: Failed
    - apiVersion: v1
      kind: ConfigMap
      name: current-config
      namespace: team-a

The operator retries deletion on the next reconcile. Anna investigates the obstacle that is blocking the delete (a rejecting webhook from another operator, or a finalizer set by another controller). Once the obstacle is removed, the orphan is cleaned up automatically.

docs.title: Scenario 4: deleting a TemplateInstance
docs.text:
Anna deletes her TemplateInstance:

kubectl delete templateinstance app -n team-a

Every resource the TemplateInstance rendered is removed from the cluster before the TemplateInstance itself is finalized. No manual cleanup is required.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Lifecycle for the cleanup model and ownership metadata.
  • Status for the meaning of status.renderedResources[].status and status.trackedGVKs.
  • API reference: ResourceReference.

docs.title: Parameter Validation
docs.text: TemplateParameterDefinition exposes four optional fields beyond name and value that let providers declare a parameter's type, whether it is required, whether the consumer is allowed to override it, and whether its resolved value is exposed in status. For the resolution model and how these fields interact with valueFrom, see Parameters.

docs.title: Fields on TemplateParameterDefinition
docs.text:
Field Type Default Purpose type enum: string, number, bool, array, object unset Validate that the literal default and any instance override parse to the declared type. required bool false When true, the consuming TemplateInstance MUST provide a value (regardless of any Template default). disableOverride bool false When true, the consuming TemplateInstance MUST NOT supply its own value for this parameter. exposeInStatus bool false When true, the resolved value is written to status.resolvedParameters[].value for inspection.

CRD-level validation rejects the conflicting combination:

required: true, disableOverride: true   # error: cannot be both required and non-overridable

docs.title: Example: a fully-described template parameter set
docs.text:
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: app-template
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: name
      type: string
      required: true
      exposeInStatus: true
    - name: replicas
      type: number
      value: "2"          # default
    - name: tlsEnabled
      type: bool
      value: "true"
    - name: dbPassword
      type: string
      required: true
      disableOverride: false   # implicit; explicit for clarity
    - name: imageRegistry
      type: string
      value: ghcr.io/stakater
      disableOverride: true     # consumers cannot change the registry
  gotemplate: |
    ...

docs.title: Type checking
docs.text:
type controls how literal strings are validated:

  • string: any value is accepted.
  • number: must parse via strconv.ParseFloat. "3", "3.14", "-2.5e10" pass; "three" fails.
  • bool: must parse via strconv.ParseBool. "true"/"false"/"1"/"0" pass; "yes" does not.

objectFieldRef may resolve to native Go types (lists, maps). When type is set to a scalar (string/number/bool), composite values are rejected: a list-valued JSONPath cannot satisfy type: string.

Type mismatches surface as:

status:
  conditions:
    - type: ParametersValid
      status: "False"
      reason: InvalidParameter
      message: "parameter \"replicas\" type mismatch: expected number, got \"two\""

docs.title: Required parameters
docs.text:
A required: true parameter:

  • Has no value default? The TemplateInstance MUST override it. A missing override sets ParametersValid=False, Reason=InvalidParameter.
  • Has a value default? The TemplateInstance MUST still override it; the default is ignored.

The intent is to force the consumer to consciously choose a value.

Usage: for environment-specific values such as database hostnames or TLS certificates. Avoid required for parameters with safe defaults.

docs.title: Locked parameters
docs.text:
disableOverride: true makes the parameter read-only from the consumer's point of view. Any TemplateInstance that tries to override surfaces:

status:
  phase: Failed
  conditions:
    - type: ParametersValid
      status: "False"
      reason: OverrideNotAllowed
      message: "parameter \"imageRegistry\" cannot be overridden by this instance"

Usage: for values the platform team owns, such as image registries, mandatory labels, or security-relevant settings.

docs.title: Status visibility
docs.text:
By default, status.resolvedParameters[] only records each parameter's name, plus the source reference for a valueFrom parameter. The resolved value itself is not written to status; useful when values are credentials.

Set exposeInStatus: true on a parameter to also record the resolved value:

status:
  resolvedParameters:
    - name: name
      value: my-app                # exposed because exposeInStatus: true
    - name: dbPassword
      valueFrom:                   # NOT exposed
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: password

Treat exposeInStatus as a public-information signal. Never set it on parameters resolved from Secret.

docs.title: Conditions and reasons
docs.text: Condition Reason When ParametersValid InvalidParameter Type mismatch on literal default; type mismatch on resolved override; missing required parameter; unknown parameter on instance. ParametersValid OverrideNotAllowed Instance attempts to override a disableOverride: true parameter. ParametersValid ParameterResolutionFailed A valueFrom source could not be resolved. ParametersValid AllParametersResolved All parameters resolved successfully.

docs.title: Adopting these fields incrementally
docs.text:
The fields are all optional with safe defaults. Adopt them incrementally:

  1. Annotate each parameter with type first; this gives you compile-time-style validation with no behavior change.
  2. Mark consumer-required values with required: true.
  3. Mark provider-owned values with disableOverride: true.
  4. Mark non-secret, audit-worthy values with exposeInStatus: true.

docs.title: Parameters and Overrides
docs.text: Examples of declaring parameters on a Template and overriding them from a TemplateInstance. For the resolution model, validation rules, namespace scoping, JSONPath syntax, watch semantics, and RBAC, see Parameters.

docs.title: Scenario 1: literal defaults overridden by the instance
docs.text:
Bill publishes a Template with literal defaults so simple consumers can use it without supplying anything.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: app-template
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: replicas
      value: "2"
    - name: image
      value: nginx:latest
    - name: env
      value: production
    - name: dbPassword
    - name: ingressIP
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: app
    spec:
      replicas: {{ .parameters.replicas }}
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: app
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: app
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: app
              image: {{ .parameters.image }}
              env:
                - name: APP_ENV
                  value: {{ .parameters.env }}
                - name: DB_PASSWORD
                  value: {{ .parameters.dbPassword | quote }}
                - name: INGRESS_IP
                  value: {{ .parameters.ingressIP | quote }}
  targetNamespaces:
    explicit:
      allow:
        literal:
          - team-a

Anna's TemplateInstance keeps the defaults except for the image:

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: app-template
    namespace: provider
  parameters:
    - name: image
      value: nginx:1.27

status.resolvedParameters lists each parameter by name. It does not record whether a literal value came from the instance or from the Template default; it shows the value only for parameters with exposeInStatus: true.

docs.title: Scenario 2: read a database password from a Secret
docs.text:
Anna's namespace already has a db-credentials Secret. She wants the TemplateInstance to read the password at render time so it doesn't appear in YAML or git history.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: team-a
type: Opaque
stringData:
  password: s3cret
---
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: app-template
    namespace: provider
  parameters:
    - name: dbPassword
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: password

The Secret value is base64-decoded automatically. With sync.mode: revert or strict, the operator subscribes to the Secret and re-reconciles the TemplateInstance whenever the password is rotated. This Template uses the default sync.mode: off, so a rotation after the first clean apply is not applied.

docs.title: Scenario 3: read the ingress IP via objectFieldRef (GET)
docs.text:
Anna wants the rendered Deployment to include the load-balancer IP of an existing Ingress. The IP is in the Ingress.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip field.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: app-template
    namespace: provider
  parameters:
    - name: ingressIP
      valueFrom:
        objectFieldRef:
          apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
          kind: Ingress
          name: my-ingress
          namespace: team-a
          jsonPath: .status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip

name is set, so this is GET mode and the result is a single string. The template uses {{ .parameters.ingressIP }} as a scalar.

docs.title: Scenario 4: list discovered services via objectFieldRef (LIST)
docs.text:
Anna wants the rendered ConfigMap to list every ConfigMap name in her namespace, no matter how many there are.

Template:

spec:
  parameters:
    - name: serviceNames
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: discovered-services
    data:
      services: |
        {{- range .parameters.serviceNames }}
        - {{ . }}
        {{- end }}

TemplateInstance:

spec:
  parameters:
    - name: serviceNames
      valueFrom:
        objectFieldRef:
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: ConfigMap
          namespace: team-a
          jsonPath: .items[*].metadata.name

Because name is omitted, this is LIST mode and serviceNames is always a list, so the template's {{ range }} is safe even when only one match is found.

docs.title: Scenario 5: fall back when the optional source is missing
docs.text:
Anna's chart can run with a default password but should pick up a real one from a Secret if it exists. She combines valueFrom with defaultValue:

spec:
  parameters:
    - name: dbPassword
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: password
      defaultValue: changeme

If db-credentials does not exist, or the password key is missing, the resolution fails and the operator uses changeme. If the Secret exists with an empty password value, the empty string is used as-is, since the resolution succeeded.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Parameters for the resolution model, type validation, watch semantics, and RBAC.
  • Parameter validation for type / required / disableOverride / exposeInStatus.
  • API reference: TemplateParameter.

docs.title: Rendering to Many Namespaces
docs.text: One TemplateInstance can render a resource into every namespace that matches a rule, and keep the set correct as namespaces come and go. This is the fan-out pattern: a single provider object, N rendered resources, reconciled on change.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Bill wants a ConfigMap called cluster-info in every namespace labelled team, and a new team namespace should get one automatically.

docs.title: 1. List the namespaces as a parameter
docs.text:
A parameter resolved from an objectFieldRef with no name runs in LIST mode: the operator lists the GVK, passes the whole list to the template, and watches it — so adding or removing a namespace re-renders the instance.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: cluster-info
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: namespaces
      required: true
  gotemplate: |
    {{- range $ns := .parameters.namespaces }}
    {{- $labels := default dict (index $ns.metadata "labels") }}
    {{- if and (hasKey $labels "team") (not (hasKey $ns.metadata "deletionTimestamp")) }}
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: cluster-info
      namespace: {{ $ns.metadata.name }}
    data:
      cluster: production
      team: {{ index $labels "team" | quote }}
    {{- end }}
    {{- end }}
  sync:
    mode: revert

The gotemplate filters in-template with hasKey/index rather than a server-side selector, so the one namespace watch covers every rule you might apply. Reading optional keys defensively matters here — see missing keys are an error.

The deletionTimestamp check skips a namespace that is being deleted. Without it, the rendered ConfigMap keeps the operator's finalizer, and the namespace stays in Terminating.

docs.title: 2. Bind it, listing all namespaces
docs.text:
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: cluster-info
  namespace: provider
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: cluster-info
    namespace: provider
  parameters:
    - name: namespaces
      valueFrom:
        objectFieldRef:
          apiVersion: v1
          kind: Namespace
          jsonPath: .items        # no name -> LIST mode, returns every Namespace

docs.title: 3. Watch it track the cluster
docs.text:
kubectl label namespace team-a team=a
kubectl label namespace team-b team=b
kubectl get configmap -A --field-selector metadata.name=cluster-info   # one per labelled namespace

kubectl create namespace team-c && kubectl label namespace team-c team=c
kubectl get configmap cluster-info -n team-c # appears without touching the TemplateInstance

docs.title: RBAC and scope
docs.text: The rendered ConfigMaps carry an explicit metadata.namespace, so the operator writes them into those namespaces — the operator's service account needs configmaps write there, and the write is not limited by targetNamespaces. Review Security → where rendered resources land before fanning out across namespaces you do not control.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Composing TemplateInstances when each item needs its own status and failure isolation.
  • Parameters: objectFieldRef GET vs LIST.

docs.title: Surfacing Status with Outputs
docs.text: A rendered resource gets values at runtime that the author never wrote — an allocated address, a generated name, a downstream controller's health. outputs lift those back onto the TemplateInstance's status, so a consumer (or another Template) can read them from one object instead of querying the rendered resources.

docs.title: Scenario 1: expose an allocated LoadBalancer IP
docs.text:
Anna renders a Service of type LoadBalancer and wants the address the cloud assigns, without running kubectl get svc herself.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: edge-service
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: name
      required: true
      exposeInStatus: true   # the output source name below reads it
  targetNamespaces:
    explicit:
      allow:
        literal:
          - consumer-a
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata:
      name: {{ .parameters.name }}
    spec:
      type: LoadBalancer
      selector:
        app: {{ .parameters.name }}
      ports:
        - port: 80
  outputs:
    - name: endpoint
      from:
        apiVersion: v1
        kind: Service
        name: "{.parameters.name}"      # JSONPath template over the Template context
      fields:
        - name: ip
          jsonPath: "{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[*].ip}"
        - name: clusterIP
          jsonPath: "{.spec.clusterIP}"

exposeInStatus matters here: under the default sync.mode: off, the instance freezes after its first apply and resolves from.name from the values recorded in status.resolvedParameters (see Sync).

Anna binds it:

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: TemplateInstance
metadata:
  name: edge-service
  namespace: consumer-a
spec:
  templateRef:
    name: edge-service
    namespace: provider
  parameters:
    - name: name
      value: edge

Once the cloud assigns an address, it appears on the instance, keyed by the Service name:

kubectl get templateinstance edge-service -n consumer-a \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.outputs}' | jq .
# { "clusterIP": { "edge": "10.96.12.34" }, "ip": { "edge": "[\"203.0.113.7\"]" } }

Until the cloud assigns an address, ip resolves to "[]" (an empty list). It does not fail the instance.

docs.title: Scenario 2: roll up the health of many rendered resources
docs.text:
When one instance renders several resources of a kind, fromAll keys an entry per resource, so the instance's status answers "is every one healthy?":

  outputs:
    - name: deployments
      fromAll:
        apiVersion: apps/v1
        kind: Deployment
      keyTemplate: "{.metadata.name}"
      fields:
        - name: available
          jsonPath: "{.status.availableReplicas}"

kubectl get templateinstance <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.outputs.available}' | jq .
# { "web": "3", "worker": "1" }

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• An array or object result is JSON-encoded into the status string ({.status.loadBalancer.ingress[*].ip} → '["203.0.113.7"]'); a scalar is stored as-is.
  • A Secret may not be an output source, so secret material can never be copied into status.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Outputs for the full semantics of from, fromAll, forEach and keyTemplate.
  • Status for where outputs sit and the OutputsResolved condition.

docs.title: Target Namespaces
docs.text: Examples of configuring Template.spec.targetNamespaces. For the matching model, default behavior, and RBAC requirements, see Target namespaces.

docs.title: Scenario 1: grant access to a fixed set of consumer namespaces
docs.text:
Bill wants team-a, team-b, and team-c to be able to instantiate his app-template. Nobody else.

apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: app-template
  namespace: provider
spec:
  gotemplate: |
    ...
  targetNamespaces:
    explicit:
      allow:
        literal:
          - team-a
          - team-b
          - team-c

A TemplateInstance created in team-a is admitted; one in team-x is rejected with TargetNamespaceAllowed=False, Reason=NamespaceNotPermitted.

docs.title: Scenario 2: grant access by namespace label
docs.text:
Bill labels every tenant namespace with kind: tenant and wants the Template available to all of them without maintaining the explicit list.

spec:
  targetNamespaces:
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        kind: tenant

The operator reads the consumer namespace's labels when it reconciles a TemplateInstance. After you add the label, a refused instance is admitted on its next retry. Removing the label does not affect an instance that is already applied until that instance reconciles again; under sync.mode: off it is frozen and is not checked again.

docs.title: Scenario 3: combine explicit and label-based access
docs.text:
Bill wants the Template available to every tenant namespace, plus the shared-platform namespace which doesn't carry the tenant label.

spec:
  targetNamespaces:
    explicit:
      allow:
        literal:
          - shared-platform
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        kind: tenant

A namespace is admitted if it matches either rule.

docs.title: Scenario 4: open the Template to every namespace
docs.text:
For a Template that's safe to instantiate anywhere (e.g. a baseline NetworkPolicy), Bill uses the wildcard:

spec:
  targetNamespaces:
    explicit:
      allow:
        literal:
          - "*"

The wildcard short-circuits all other matching. Use it deliberately.

docs.title: What a refusal looks like
docs.text:
When Anna creates a TemplateInstance in a non-permitted namespace, the operator publishes:

status:
  phase: Failed
  conditions:
    - type: TargetNamespaceAllowed
      status: "False"
      reason: NamespaceNotPermitted
      message: |
        Namespace team-x is not permitted to instantiate Template provider/app-template.
        Check Template's targetNamespaces configuration
    - type: Ready
      status: "False"
      reason: NamespaceNotPermitted

Fixing the policy on the Template, or moving the TemplateInstance to a permitted namespace, triggers the next reconcile and clears the condition.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Target namespaces for the matching model and RBAC.
  • API reference: TargetNamespaces.

docs.title: Testing Templates
docs.text:
A Template's gotemplate is code, and it is rendered by the operator — not by Helm and not by your shell. Test it the way the operator runs it, so a template that passes your tests behaves the same on the cluster. Four layers, each catching what the one above structurally cannot.

Layer Needs Catches Chart/YAML lint nothing malformed Template YAML Render tests Go, no cluster wrong rendered output, over any input you choose Admission tests envtest + the CRDs Template/TemplateInstance the API server would reject (schema + CEL) End-to-end a kind cluster + the operator what actually happens once resources are applied

docs.title: Render tests: use the operator's engine, not Helm
docs.text:
The operator renders with Go text/template plus Sprig's TxtFuncMap minus env, expandenv, getHostByName, and with the missingkey=error option. Helm is different — it adds toYaml/include/tpl/.Files and replaces fromJson/toJson — so a gotemplate can pass under Helm and fail on the cluster. Mirror the operator's engine exactly:

package render

import (
    "bytes"
    "text/template"

    "github.com/Masterminds/sprig/v3"
)

// funcs mirrors the operator's function map: Sprig minus the three removed for safety.
func funcs() template.FuncMap {
    f := sprig.TxtFuncMap()
    delete(f, "env")
    delete(f, "expandenv")
    delete(f, "getHostByName")
    return f
}

// Render executes a gotemplate the way the operator does.
func Render(src string, params map[string]any) (string, error) {
    t, err := template.New("t").Funcs(funcs()).Option("missingkey=error").Parse(src)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    var out bytes.Buffer
    ctx := map[string]any{"parameters": params, "instance": map[string]any{"name": "x", "namespace": "x"}}
    err = t.Execute(&out, ctx)
    return out.String(), err
}

missingkey=error is the part a Helm-based test would miss — see missing keys are an error and this is Sprig, not Helm.

Then table-drive it against the shapes your inputs really take — an object with the key present, absent, and null; an empty LIST; a value a consumer controls:

func TestRender(t *testing.T) {
    cases := []struct{ name string; params map[string]any; wantErr bool }{
        {"has label", map[string]any{"ns": map[string]any{"metadata": map[string]any{"labels": map[string]any{"team": "a"}}}}, false},
        {"no labels", map[string]any{"ns": map[string]any{"metadata": map[string]any{}}}, false},   // must not panic/err
    }
    for _, tc := range cases {
        t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            _, err := Render(src, tc.params)
            if (err != nil) != tc.wantErr {
                t.Fatalf("err=%v want %v", err, tc.wantErr)
            }
        })
    }
}

A test that cannot fail proves nothing: break a guard on purpose and confirm the matching case goes red.

docs.title: Admission tests: will the API server accept the CR?
docs.text: Render tests prove the output is right; they do not prove the Template or TemplateInstance CR will be accepted. Stand up an API server with envtest, install the operator's CRDs, and apply the objects your chart produces. This catches structural-schema violations and the CEL rules on the CRDs that only the API server enforces. Vendor the CRDs at the operator version you support, and refresh them when you upgrade (see Versioning and compatibility).

docs.title: End-to-end: run it against the operator
docs.text: Finally, run on a kind cluster with the operator installed: apply the Template and TemplateInstance, wait for Ready, and assert on what was rendered and on the status (outputs, conditions). This is the only layer that exercises apply, drift (sync) and cleanup (lifecycle).

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Gotemplate — the engine and its gotchas.
  • Parameter validation — declaring types and required/locked parameters so bad input is rejected early.
  • Versioning and compatibility — pinning the version you test against.

docs.title: Using Go Templates
docs.text: spec.gotemplate is an inline Go template that renders into one or more Kubernetes manifests. It uses Go's text/template syntax with Sprig functions.

docs.title: Template variables
docs.text:
The following variables are available inside the template:

Path Description .parameters.<name> Resolved value for parameter <name>. .instance.name Name of the consuming TemplateInstance. .instance.namespace Namespace of the consuming TemplateInstance. .instance.labels The TemplateInstance's labels, as a map.

docs.title: Example: ConfigMap and Service
docs.text:
apiVersion: templates.v2.stakater.com/v2alpha1
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: app-bundle
  namespace: provider
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: name
    - name: port
      value: "8080"
    - name: env
      value: production
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: {{ .parameters.name }}-config
      labels:
        app: {{ .parameters.name }}
        env: {{ .parameters.env }}
    data:
      PORT: "{{ .parameters.port }}"
      INSTANCE: {{ .instance.name }}
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata:
      name: {{ .parameters.name }}
    spec:
      selector:
        app: {{ .parameters.name }}
      ports:
        - port: {{ .parameters.port }}
          targetPort: {{ .parameters.port }}

A single gotemplate may emit any number of manifests separated by ---. The operator parses each non-empty document as one rendered resource.

docs.title: Default namespace handling
docs.text: If a rendered manifest omits metadata.namespace for a namespaced resource, the operator sets it to the TemplateInstance's namespace before applying. Cluster-scoped resources (e.g. ClusterRole, Namespace) are applied as-is.

docs.title: Sprig examples
docs.text:
spec:
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: {{ .parameters.name | lower }}-config
      labels:
        app: {{ .parameters.name | lower }}
    data:
      uppercased: {{ .parameters.name | upper | quote }}
      generated: {{ now | date "2006-01-02" }}
      hash: {{ .parameters.name | sha256sum | trunc 8 }}

docs.title: Iterating over list-valued parameters
docs.text:
When a parameter is resolved via objectFieldRef in LIST mode, the value is always a list. Iterate with range:

spec:
  parameters:
    - name: serviceNames
  gotemplate: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap
    metadata:
      name: discovered-services
    data:
      services: |
        {{- range .parameters.serviceNames }}
        - {{ . }}
        {{- end }}

docs.title: Validation behavior
docs.text:
When the Template is created or updated, the controller:

  1. Parses the template string. A parse error sets Valid=False, Reason=ValidationFailed.
  2. If every parameter has a literal value, the controller dry-run renders the template with those values and validates the YAML output. Any rendering or YAML validation error sets DryRunRendered=False, Reason=RenderFailed.
  3. If even one parameter is dynamic (no literal value), the dry-run is skipped and the controller sets DryRunRendered=False, Reason=DryRunSkipped. The Template is still considered Valid overall.

This means a Template with parameters that are resolved at the TemplateInstance level will not be dry-run rendered at template-creation time. The first end-to-end validation happens when the first TemplateInstance is created.

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text:
• The output must be parseable as YAML once rendered.
  • Each top-level manifest must be a valid Kubernetes object (have apiVersion, kind, metadata.name).
  • Empty documents between --- separators are skipped.

docs.title: Benefits of Template Operator v2
docs.text: Template Operator v2 lets a platform team define reusable template artifacts (Go templates or Helm charts) that consumer teams instantiate into their own namespaces with their own parameters. The operator handles rendering, applying, finalization, and clean-up.

docs.title: 1. Author once, instantiate many
docs.text: Platform teams maintain a single Template in their provider namespace. Any number of TemplateInstance resources, in any permitted consumer namespace, can render that Template with their own parameter overrides.

docs.title: 2. Two rendering engines
docs.text: A Template is either a Go template (spec.gotemplate), with the full Go text/template syntax plus a sandboxed Sprig function set, or a Helm chart (spec.helm) pulled from an HTTP, HTTPS, or OCI repository. Exactly one is required; the API forbids both. The same parameter machinery feeds either engine.

docs.title: 3. Parameter resolution at render time
docs.text:
Parameter overrides on a TemplateInstance can be:

  • Literal strings.
  • valueFrom.secretKeyRef / configMapKeyRef, resolves a key from a Secret or ConfigMap at render time.
  • valueFrom.objectFieldRef, resolves a JSONPath against any cluster resource by GVK, in either GET (named resource) or LIST (all resources of a kind, with wildcards) mode.

Note

Resolution is fail-fast: if any single parameter can't be resolved, the instance does not render with partial values.

docs.title: 4. Namespace-scoped authorization
docs.text: A Template's targetNamespaces field controls which consumer namespaces are allowed to instantiate it. The default, when targetNamespaces is omitted, is that only TemplateInstances in the Template's own namespace are permitted. An explicit allow-list, a namespace label selector, or the wildcard * opens it up further.

docs.title: 5. Standard Kubernetes status reporting
docs.text: Every CR follows Kubernetes status conventions: a phase, an observedGeneration, and a list of conditions with Reason and Message. There is no operator-specific status format to learn, kubectl describe, kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready, and tools like ArgoCD integrate naturally.

docs.title: 6. Rendered-resource lifecycle is tracked
docs.text: The operator stamps each rendered resource with a finalizer and records its apiVersion, kind, name, and namespace in status.renderedResources. Deleting the TemplateInstance cleanly removes every rendered resource. With sync.mode: revert or strict, updating a Template to render a smaller set causes orphans to be deleted on the next reconcile.

docs.title: 7. GitOps-friendly
docs.text: Both CRs are plain Kubernetes resources with declarative spec. Anything you can express in YAML you can manage with Argo CD, Flux, or kubectl apply -f.

docs.title: Two template engines
docs.text: A Template exposes exactly one of two engines, enforced by an API-level validation rule (has(self.gotemplate) != has(self.helm)).

docs.title: Go template
docs.text: spec.gotemplate is a string parsed with Go's text/template plus Sprig functions. The output may emit one or more Kubernetes manifests separated by YAML document markers. The following Sprig functions are removed for safety: env, expandenv, getHostByName.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
spec.helm references a chart by repository URL, chart name, and SemVer 2 version:

  • HTTP/HTTPS repositories: url: https://charts.example.com
  • OCI registries: url: oci://ghcr.io/org/charts

Both Helm v3 and v4 SDKs are bundled. Pick with spec.helm.version: v3 or v4. When omitted, v3 is the default. Optional spec.helm.valuesTemplate is itself a Go template that, after rendering, is parsed as YAML and merged over the chart's default values.

Private repositories are supported via spec.helm.chart.repository.auth.secretRef, which references a Secret in the Template's namespace (not the consumer's).

docs.title: Available data
docs.text:
Both engines see the same context object:

  • .parameters, the resolved parameter map.
  • .instance.name, .instance.namespace, .instance.labels, metadata of the consuming TemplateInstance.

Important

If a rendered manifest omits metadata.namespace, the operator sets it to the TemplateInstance's namespace before applying.

docs.title: Dynamic parameter resolution
docs.text:
TemplateInstance parameter overrides may resolve their value at render time:

Source Field Reads Secret valueFrom.secretKeyRef A specific key, base64-decoded ConfigMap valueFrom.configMapKeyRef A specific key Any resource valueFrom.objectFieldRef A JSONPath expression evaluated against the resource (GET mode) or against a list of resources (LIST mode, when name is omitted)

objectFieldRef returns a scalar in GET mode; it always returns a list in LIST mode so templates can {{range}} safely. With sync.mode: revert or strict, the operator dynamically watches every resource referenced by valueFrom, and re-reconciles the TemplateInstance when the source changes.

A defaultValue may be set on each TemplateInstance parameter; it is used only when paired with valueFrom, and applies whenever the valueFrom resolution fails (missing resource, missing key, JSONPath error, and so on).

docs.title: Target namespace control
docs.text:
Template.spec.targetNamespaces decides which consumer namespaces are allowed to instantiate the Template:

  • Omitted entirely → same namespace as the Template only (default).
  • explicit.allow.literal: ["*"] → all namespaces.
  • explicit.allow.literal: [...] → explicit allow-list.
  • selector → namespaces whose labels match the LabelSelector.
  • A namespace is permitted if it matches the explicit list or the selector.

If a TemplateInstance is created in a non-permitted namespace, the controller sets the TargetNamespaceAllowed condition to False and refuses to render.

docs.title: Lifecycle and clean-up
docs.text:
• Every rendered resource carries a finalizer (templates.v2.stakater.com/template-instance-resource) so the operator can clean up before the API server garbage-collects.
  • Template deletion is blocked while any TemplateInstance references it, the controller publishes the Deleting condition with reason DeletionBlocked.
  • TemplateInstance deletion sweeps every resource recorded in status.renderedResources, removes the finalizer, then removes its own finalizer.

docs.title: Status reporting
docs.text:
Every CR exposes:

  • status.phase, Valid/Invalid/Error for Template; Ready/Failed for TemplateInstance.
  • status.observedGeneration, last metadata.generation reconciled.
  • status.conditions[], Kubernetes-standard with Type, Status, Reason, Message, LastTransitionTime, ObservedGeneration.

TemplateInstance additionally exposes:

  • status.resolvedParameters, the source map for each parameter after merging defaults and overrides.
  • status.renderedResources, identity (apiVersion/kind/name/namespace) plus per-resource observedGeneration and status (empty for successfully applied, Failed when the operator is retrying) for every applied resource.
  • status.resolvedTemplateRef, the name/namespace/generation of the Template that was actually rendered.

docs.title: Validation at template-creation time
docs.text:
The Template controller dry-run renders new and updated templates as soon as they are created. For Helm templates this includes pulling the chart, verifying the source is reachable, and rendering with the valuesTemplate output. The result is reported via:

  • Valid, template spec parses and renders.
  • SourceAccessible, for Helm: chart could be pulled.
  • DryRunRendered, render produces valid YAML.

Dry-run is skipped when any parameter has no literal default value (since the runtime type cannot be guessed safely).
